## 4. Asymptotics: the late tail decays like $1/\log B_1$

Section 3 is a numerical instance. We now remove the numerics.

> **Lemma 4.1 (Late primes divide the primorial).** $\prod_{p \in \mathcal{L}(B_1,y)} p$ divides the primorial $B_1\# = \prod_{p \le B_1} p$.

> **Theorem 4.2 (Chebyshev-type count of the late schedule).** For $y \ge 2$,
> $$\#\mathcal{L}(B_1,y)\cdot \lfloor \log_2 y\rfloor \;\le\; 2 B_1 .$$

*Proof.* Write $k = \#\mathcal{L}(B_1,y)$. Every late prime exceeds $y$, so $y^{k} \le \prod_{p\in\mathcal{L}} p$. By Lemma 4.1 and Erdős' bound $B_1\# \le 4^{B_1}$, that product is at most $4^{B_1}$. Also $2^{\lfloor \log_2 y\rfloor} \le y$. Chaining,
$$2^{k\lfloor \log_2 y\rfloor} = \big(2^{\lfloor\log_2 y\rfloor}\big)^{k} \le y^{k} \le \prod_{p \in \mathcal{L}} p \le 4^{B_1} = 2^{2B_1},$$
and comparing exponents of $2$ gives the claim. $\square$

> **Lemma 4.3.** $\displaystyle\sum_{p \in \mathcal{L}(B_1,y)} \frac{1}{p} \;\le\; \frac{\#\mathcal{L}(B_1,y)}{y}$, since each late prime exceeds $y$.

> **Theorem 4.4 (Unconditional late-density bound).** For all $M, B_1$ and every cut $y \ge 2$,
> $$\#\,\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{late}}(M,B_1,y) \;\le\; \frac{2 M B_1}{y\,\lfloor \log_2 y\rfloor}.$$

*Proof.* Theorem 3.2 gives $\#\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{late}} \le M\sum_{p\in\mathcal L} 1/p$; Lemma 4.3 bounds the sum by $\#\mathcal{L}/y$; Theorem 4.2 bounds $\#\mathcal{L}$ by $2B_1/\lfloor\log_2 y\rfloor$. $\square$

> **Corollary 4.5 (No constant-fraction late tail).** If the cut is at half the stage-one bound, $B_1 \le 2y$, then
> $$\frac{\#\,\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{late}}(M,B_1,y)}{M} \;\le\; \frac{4}{\lfloor \log_2 y\rfloor} \;\xrightarrow[\;y\to\infty\;]{}\; 0 .$$
> In particular no fixed positive fraction — such as H1's $20\%$ — can be the late tail for all large $B_1$.

> **Example 4.6.** At $B_1 = 2^{20}$ with the cut at $y = 2^{19}$, Corollary 4.5 gives a late density below $4/19 \approx 0.2105$; at $B_1 = 2^{26}$, below $0.16$; at $B_1 = 2^{32}$, below $0.129$. The bound is deliberately crude (it discards the sparsity of primes beyond the Erdős estimate) but its *direction* is unconditional: the ceiling descends like the reciprocal of a logarithm.

---

## 5. Model discrimination: integer model versus divisor model

Theorems 3.5 and 4.4 are statements about a specific null model — the order is a uniform *integer* in $(0,M]$. The competing model, implicit whenever one says "the accounting is collision-dominated", takes the order to be a uniform *divisor of $K(B_1)$*. That model is computable exactly, and it predicts the opposite.

> **Theorem 5.1 (Divisor firing set).** For all $B_1, y$,
> $$\{d \mid K(B_1) : P^{+}(d) \le y\} \;=\; \{d : d \mid K(B_1,y)\}.$$
> That is, the divisors of the full multiplier that fire by position $y$ are exactly the divisors of the partial multiplier.

*Proof.* Immediate from Theorem 2.7 in both directions, using that $K(B_1,y) \mid K(B_1)$ (which follows from $K(B_1,y) = K(B_1,\min(y,B_1))$ and monotonicity of the index set). $\square$

> **Lemma 5.2 (Divisor count of a squarefree-indexed prime-power product).** For a finite set $S$ of primes and any exponent function $e : S \to \mathbb{N}$,
> $$\tau\Big(\prod_{p\in S} p^{e(p)}\Big) = \prod_{p \in S} \big(e(p)+1\big).$$

> **Theorem 5.3 (Divisor-model firing law).** For all $B_1, y$,
> $$\tau\big(K(B_1)\big) \;=\; \tau\big(K(B_1,y)\big)\cdot \prod_{p \in \mathcal{L}(B_1,y)} \big(\lfloor \log_p B_1\rfloor + 1\big).$$
> Equivalently, a uniformly random divisor of $K(B_1)$ fires by position $y$ with probability exactly
> $$\Big(\prod_{p \in \mathcal{L}(B_1,y)} \big(\lfloor\log_p B_1\rfloor+1\big)\Big)^{-1}.$$

*Proof.* Split $\mathcal{P}(B_1) = \mathcal{P}(\min(y,B_1)) \sqcup \mathcal{L}(B_1,y)$; the two resulting factors of $K(B_1)$ are coprime, so $\tau$ is multiplicative across them; apply Lemma 5.2 to the late factor and Theorem 5.1 to identify the early factor with $\tau(K(B_1,y))$. $\square$

> **Corollary 5.4 (The divisor model fires late).** At $B_1 = 100$, $y = 67$: each of the six late primes has $\lfloor \log_p 100\rfloor = 1$, so the local factor is $2^{6} = 64$ and
> $$\tau\big(K(100)\big) = 64 \cdot \tau\big(K(100,67)\big), \qquad \frac{\tau(K(100,67))}{\tau(K(100))} = \frac{1}{64}.$$
> The divisor model therefore places $63/64 = 98.44\%$ of its firing mass in the final six schedule steps. (Numerically $\tau(K(100)) = 660{,}602{,}880$ and $\tau(K(100,67)) = 10{,}321{,}920$.)

> **Theorem 5.5 (Discrimination).** On the single observable measured — the mass in the final six of the twenty-five schedule steps at $B_1 = 100$ — the integer model caps the mass at $2/25 = 0.08$ (Theorem 3.5) while the divisor model requires $63/64 = 0.984$. Since $12 \cdot (2/25) < 63/64$, the two null models differ by more than a factor of twelve, and the observable is decisive between them.

> **Corollary 5.6 (Verdict).** The measured empty tail has likelihood $(1/64)^{55} \approx 4.6\times10^{-100}$ under the divisor model, versus $\ge 10^{-2}$ under the integer model. The order of a point on a random curve behaves, as far as the firing trace is concerned, like a random *integer* below $B_1$, not like a random *divisor* of the stage-one multiplier. The early-fire signature is the $\pi$-compression of a typical largest prime factor.

This is worth emphasising as a methodological point: the trace observable was designed to test a hypothesis about *timing*, and it happens also to be a sharp discriminator between two natural priors on the order. Negative results about the registered hypotheses are thus accompanied by a positive result about model selection.

---

## 6. The collision baseline: refutation of H2

### 6.1 The ceiling

> **Definition 6.1.** The *collision probability* of a run of $k$ guarded group operations modulo $p$ is $\mathrm{coll}(p,k) := 1 - (1 - 1/p)^{k}$: the chance that some intermediate quantity is accidentally divisible by $p$, irrespective of the point's order.

> **Theorem 6.2 (Bernoulli ceiling).** For every prime $p$ and every $k \ge 0$, $\mathrm{coll}(p,k) \le k/p$.

*Proof.* Bernoulli's inequality $(1+x)^{k} \ge 1 + kx$ holds for $x \ge -2$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$; apply it with $x = -1/p \ge -1$, so $(1-1/p)^{k} \ge 1 - k/p$, i.e. $1 - (1-1/p)^{k} \le k/p$. $\square$

### 6.2 Scale freedom, and why H2 was untestable as posed

> **Theorem 6.3 (Scale freedom).** If $k/p = \ell/q$ then $\mathrm{coll}(p,k) \le \ell/q$ and $\mathrm{coll}(q,\ell) \le k/p$: the ceiling is a function of the ratio alone.

The consequence is structural. In the experiment, the operation count is $k = c\,B_1$ and the design fixes $B_1/p$; hence $k/p = c\,(B_1/p)$ is *invariant* across bit lengths by construction. A collision-dominated account therefore predicts **the same** ceiling at $26$ bits and at $32$ bits. H2 asserted that the observed rate should collapse toward the floor as the bit length grows; but the floor does not move, so no such collapse is implied by the collision hypothesis in the first place. The measured flatness — $65.0\%$ versus $62.5\%$, two-proportion $z$-test $p = 0.8161$ — is exactly what *both* hypotheses predict, and therefore discriminates neither. H2 is not merely false: as posed, it was not a test.

What *does* discriminate is the level.

### 6.3 The level: collisions are subdominant

The pre-registration used $c = 1.44$, giving a per-curve floor of $1 - \exp(-1.44 \cdot 0.125) = 16.47\%$. Auditing the implementation showed the true operation count is $c = 2.59$ per unit of $B_1$; we recompute both ways and report both. With $c = 2.59$ and $B_1/p = 0.125$,
$$\frac{k}{p} = 2.59 \times 0.125 = 0.32375 \;<\; 0.324,$$
so by Theorem 6.2 the per-curve collision probability is at most $0.324$ for *every* prime $p$. (Exponential-model per-curve means are $27.1$–$27.8\%$; three-curve cell means under exact-op collision arithmetic are $61.2$–$62.3\%$, coincidentally close to the measured cell rates — a coincidence we flag explicitly below.)

> **Theorem 6.4 (Subdominance).** If $k \le 0.324\,p$ and the observed per-curve success rate satisfies $\mathrm{obs} \ge 0.625$, then $\mathrm{coll}(p,k) + 0.3 \le \mathrm{obs}$.

*Proof.* $\mathrm{coll}(p,k) \le k/p \le 0.324$ by Theorem 6.2, and $0.324 + 0.3 = 0.624 \le 0.625 \le \mathrm{obs}$. $\square$

### 6.4 Pigeonhole: genuine order-hits must exist

> **Theorem 6.5.** Let $S$ be the set of successful curves in a batch and $C$ the set of collision-driven ones. Then $\#(S\setminus C) \ge \#S - \#C$.

*Proof.* $S \subseteq (S\setminus C)\cup C$, so $\#S \le \#(S\setminus C)+\#C$. $\square$

> **Corollary 6.6 (The measured cell).** In a cell of $40$ curves with $25$ successes, at most $\lfloor 0.324\cdot 40\rfloor = 12$ can be collision-driven, so at least $\mathbf{13}$ successes are genuine order-hits.

**Verdict on H2.** Collisions are real and non-negligible — they account for up to a third of per-curve successes at the operating point — but they are *subdominant*, and the low-$B_1$ successes cannot be explained away as collision luck. Moreover the collision hypothesis is structurally incapable of predicting the cross-scale collapse H2 asserted.

---

## 7. Computation

We report direct computation over uniform orders, taking $B_1 = N$ and letting $n$ range over all integers in $(0,N]$, with the firing index $\pi(P^{+}(n))/\pi(N)$ evaluated by a largest-prime-factor sieve (cost $O(N\log\log N)$).

| $N$ | schedule steps $\pi(N)$ | median index | mean index | final-$20\%$ mass | first-$20\%$ mass |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| $10^{3}$ | $168$ | $0.083$ | $0.176$ | $3.4\%$ | $73.0\%$ |
| $10^{4}$ | $1229$ | $0.035$ | $0.122$ | $2.5\%$ | $81.7\%$ |
| $10^{5}$ | $9592$ | $0.014$ | $0.091$ | $1.9\%$ | $86.3\%$ |
| $10^{6}$ | $78498$ | $0.006$ | $0.072$ | $1.6\%$ | $89.0\%$ |

A uniform firing index would produce $0.500$ in both the median and mean columns and $20.0\%$ in both mass columns. Instead:

* the median firing index tends to zero — consistent with the measured medians $0.09$–$0.102$ at the (much smaller) $B_1$ of the live experiment;
* the final-$20\%$ mass decays monotonically, in line with Corollary 4.5;
* the first-$20\%$ mass rises toward $90\%$: the trace is overwhelmingly an early-fire phenomenon.

Direct verification of the trace law on all $(\text{divisor}, \text{cut})$ pairs for $B_1 \in \{12, 20, 30\}$ — $576$, $8640$ and $84{,}480$ pairs respectively — records zero violations, as Theorem 2.7 requires.

---

## 8. Discussion

### 8.1 Why the intuition failed

The intuition behind H1 was that "order completion takes the whole schedule". It is a natural picture and it is wrong for a specific reason: the accumulated scalar is not accreting the order's factors one at a time in a race against the schedule's end. By the time the walk has passed a prime $p$, the scalar already contains $p$ to the *maximum* exponent stage one will ever supply. So a reachable order is satisfied the instant its largest prime factor has been passed — and largest prime factors of typical integers are small. The $\pi$-rescaling then amplifies the effect enormously, because prime density falls off: passing from step $\pi(y)$ to $\pi(2y)$ costs many schedule steps but adds only sparse, high primes, which few orders need.

### 8.2 The trace law as a bridge

Theorem 2.7 has a use beyond refutation. It says the firing trace is an *observable of $P^{+}$*, so any classical result about the distribution of the largest prime factor becomes a prediction about the algorithm's runtime profile, and conversely any measured trace becomes an empirical probe of $P^{+}$ statistics on the arithmetically constrained population of elliptic-curve group orders. The Dickman function $\rho$, which governs $\Pr[P^{+}(n) \le n^{1/u}] \to \rho(u)$, and Golomb's results on the largest-prime-factor distribution, are the natural asymptotic inputs; Theorem 3.3 shows the finite-range problem is *exactly* a truncated Mertens sum.

### 8.3 Honest caveats

Several limitations are inherent to the measurement and are stated here so that the structural theorems are not over-read.

1. **Operation-count constant.** The pre-registered baseline used $c = 1.44$; the honest count is $c = 2.59$. All baselines are recomputed both ways and both are reported. The corrected floor is higher and correspondingly weakens — but does not overturn — the excess argument of Section 6.
2. **Numerical coincidence.** Under exact-operation collision arithmetic, three-curve cell means come out at $61.2$–$62.3\%$, uncomfortably close to the measured cell rates. This coincidence is flagged rather than suppressed. The per-curve excess (Theorem 6.4), the trace-shape rejection, and the empty late tail are what rule out collision dominance; the cell-level rate alone would not.
3. **Censoring.** Successes attributable purely to the second cofactor are censored from the accounting and are not counted as order-hits; this is a conservative choice that, if anything, understates the order-hit fraction.
4. **Silent failure mode.** One class of degenerate curves collapses without a diagnostic; this behaviour is inherited from the parent experimental design and is not re-derived here.
5. **Bound crudeness.** Corollary 4.5 discards prime sparsity beyond the Erdős estimate; the true decay is expected to be governed by the Mertens law of Section 9, which is sharper by a constant factor and matches computation closely.
6. **Independence in the likelihood computation.** Proposition 3.7 treats the $55$ hits as independent Bernoulli trials, which is the same assumption the pre-registered binomial test made; correlations induced by shared curve parameters would inflate both likelihoods but not, to first order, their ratio.

### 8.4 A caught error, reported

During instrumentation the closed-form step counter — used to cross-check the traced counter — was initially wrong on later chunks of the schedule: the relevant length *doubles* and the population count *adds*, rather than the off-by-one behaviour first coded. The discrepancy was caught by an assertion comparing traced against closed-form counts *before any full dataset existed*, fixed, and re-verified against $29$ of $29$ smoke curves; smoke data were regenerated after the fix. No result in this paper depends on the pre-fix counter.

### 8.5 Where this sits

This work is an audit that closes an evidence chain rather than a breach of any barrier. An earlier finding — that no abrupt destruction threshold appears in the parameter regime studied — was challenged on the grounds that its accounting conflated smoothness hits with collisions. The proposed amendment is rejected here, on two independent grounds (level and trace shape), and the earlier no-threshold account stands unamended. No constant is improved and no complexity claim is made. What is new is the trace law and the family of bounds it generates.

---

## 9. Future work

### 9.1 The Mertens Firing-Tail Law (conjecture)

Cut the schedule at the $(1-\tau)$-quantile, i.e. at $y$ with $\pi(y) = (1-\tau)\pi(B_1)$. By Theorem 3.3 the late-firing density in the short range is the truncated reciprocal sum $\sum_{y<p\le B_1} 1/p$, and Mertens' second theorem evaluates it as $\log\log B_1 - \log\log y + o(1)$. With $y \approx B_1^{1-\tau'}$ for the corresponding logarithmic scale, this suggests:

> **Conjecture 9.1 (Mertens Firing-Tail Law).**
> $$\mathrm{tail}(\tau, B_1) \;=\; \frac{\log\big(1/(1-\tau)\big)}{\log B_1}\,\big(1 + o(1)\big) \qquad (B_1 \to \infty).$$

At $\tau = 0.2$ the numerator is $\log(1.25) = 0.2231$, and the prediction against the computed table of Section 7 is:

| $B_1$ | predicted $\mathrm{tail}(0.2)$ | measured |
|---:|---:|---:|
| $10^{3}$ | $0.0323$ | $0.0340$ |
| $10^{4}$ | $0.0242$ | $0.0250$ |
| $10^{5}$ | $0.0194$ | $0.0190$ |
| $10^{6}$ | $0.0162$ | $0.0160$ |

Agreement to within a few thousandths across three orders of magnitude. Proving Conjecture 9.1 requires (i) an effective form of Mertens' theorem over the truncated range, (ii) control of the $\pi$-quantile-to-value conversion, and (iii) an inclusion–exclusion correction beyond the short range $M \le y^{2}$, where multiple large prime divisors become possible.

### 9.2 Further directions

* **Beyond the short range.** Theorem 3.3 is exact only for $M \le y^{2}$. A second-order inclusion–exclusion term $-\sum_{y<p<q\le B_1}\lfloor M/pq\rfloor$ should extend exactness to $M \le y^{3}$, and a full Legendre-type expansion should give the tail to all orders.
* **Sharpening the Chebyshev input.** Replacing Erdős' $4^{B_1}$ by an effective Chebyshev bound $\theta(x) < 1.001102\,x$ would improve the constant in Theorem 4.4 from $2$ to roughly $1.45/\log 2$, tightening Corollary 4.5.
* **Stage two.** The continuation phase of the elliptic-curve method admits a single extra large prime beyond $B_1$; the trace law should extend to a two-parameter statement in which the firing threshold is $\max(P^{+}_{(2)}(n), \text{second-largest})$, with the late tail governed by a two-dimensional Dickman-type region.
* **Order-population bias.** Elliptic-curve group orders are not uniform integers: they are biased by torsion structure and by the curve's construction. Quantifying the deviation of $P^{+}$ statistics on that population from the uniform-integer baseline would sharpen every density estimate here.
* **Early-abort scheduling.** If nine-tenths of the firing mass lies in the first fifth of the schedule, a practical implication follows: a *fractional* stage-one run at $B_1$ captures most of the hits of a full run, and the optimal allocation of a fixed operation budget across curves and schedule fractions is a concrete optimization problem the trace law makes tractable.
* **Trace as a diagnostic.** Because the firing index reads off $\pi(P^{+}(n))/\pi(B_1)$, an observed trace is a direct measurement of the largest prime factor of the hidden group order — usable as a runtime diagnostic to re-tune $B_1$ adaptively mid-computation.

---

## 10. Conclusion

The moment at which the first stage of the elliptic-curve method succeeds is not a complicated function of the run. It is the largest prime factor of the point's order, read through the prime-counting function. From that single identity follow: the structural thinness of the late tail (below $8\%$ at $B_1 = 100$, versus $20$–$24\%$ under uniformity), its unconditional decay like $1/\log$, the exact firing law of the competing divisor model and its refutation by more than a factor of twelve, and — on the rate side — the scale freedom of the collision baseline that renders a bit-length-collapse hypothesis untestable, together with a level gap of thirty percentage points that pigeonholes into at least thirteen genuine order-hits per measured cell.

Two pre-registered hypotheses died. The replacement is not another statistical claim but a theorem, and it points at one of the oldest questions in multiplicative number theory: how big is the biggest prime in a random integer? Almost always, small — which is precisely why this clock always strikes early.

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The question}

The elliptic-curve method of factorization is a sub-exponential algorithm whose
running time is governed by the density of smooth numbers. Given a composite
$N$ with an unknown prime factor $p$, one selects a random elliptic curve $E$
over $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ and a point $P$ on it, and computes
$K(B_1)\cdot P$, where
\[
  K(B_1)\;=\;\prod_{p'\le B_1}(p')^{\lfloor \log_{p'}B_1\rfloor}.
\]
If the order $n$ of $P$ in $E(\mathbb{F}_p)$ divides $K(B_1)$, then
$K(B_1)\cdot P$ is the identity modulo $p$ but typically not modulo other prime
factors of $N$; the projective arithmetic then requires the inverse of a
quantity divisible by $p$, and a greatest-common-divisor computation exposes
$p$. By Hasse's theorem $|\#E(\mathbb{F}_p)-p-1|\le 2\sqrt{p}$, so the success
probability per curve is essentially the probability that a random integer near
$p$ is $B_1$-smooth.

The literature is rich on \emph{whether} and \emph{how often} a curve succeeds.
It is essentially silent on \emph{when within a run} it succeeds. Since stage
one is implemented as a walk over the schedule
$p_1<p_2<\dots<p_{\pi(B_1)}$, multiplying by $p_i^{\lfloor\log_{p_i}B_1\rfloor}$
at step $i$, each successful curve carries a \emph{firing index}: the fraction
of the schedule consumed at the moment the point died.

\subsection{The pre-registered hypotheses}

\paragraph{H1 (trace shape).} At small $B_1/p$, successes are dominated by
accidental arithmetic collisions, which strike uniformly through the run, so
the firing index should be \emph{uniform} on $[0,1]$. At large $B_1/p$,
successes reflect genuine \emph{order completion}, which should require most of
the schedule, so the firing index should concentrate in the \emph{final} $20\%$.

\paragraph{H2 (rate collapse).} Guarded projective accounting carries a
random-collision baseline of roughly $1-\exp(-cB_1/p)$ per curve. If the
low-$B_1$ successes are collision luck, then holding $B_1/p$ fixed and
increasing the bit length of $p$ should drive the observed success rate down
toward that baseline.

\subsection{Results}

Both hypotheses fail, and H1 fails with \emph{inverted geometry}. Measured
medians of the normalized firing index at $B_1/p=0.9$ are $0.09$ and $0.102$ at
bit lengths $26$ and $32$; the final-$20\%$ tail contains $0$ of $55$ recorded
hits (binomial $p\approx 0.004$); and a Kolmogorov--Smirnov test rejects
uniformity even at $B_1/p=0.125$ ($p=0.0166$ and $0.0446$). On the rate side,
measured per-cell success rates at $B_1/p=0.125$ are $65.0\%$ (bit length $26$,
CI $[0.495,0.779]$) and $62.5\%$ (bit length $32$, CI $[0.470,0.758]$), far
above the per-curve collision floor of $16.47\%$ computed with the registered
constant $c=1.44$ and above the corrected floor of $27.1$--$27.8\%$ using the
honest count $k=2.59\,B_1$, with no cross-scale drift (two-proportion $z$-test,
$p=0.8161$). This paper supplies the \emph{structural} explanation.

\section{The stage-one schedule and the trace law}

Throughout, $p$ and $q$ denote primes, $\pi(x)$ is the prime-counting function,
and $\lfloor\log_p B_1\rfloor$ is the largest $e$ with $p^{e}\le B_1$.

\begin{definition}[Schedule prefix]
For $y\ge 0$, $\mathcal{P}(y):=\{p\le y: p \text{ prime}\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Partial stage-one multiplier]
$K(B_1,y):=\prod_{p\in\mathcal{P}(y)}p^{\lfloor\log_p B_1\rfloor}$, and
$K(B_1):=K(B_1,B_1)$. Primes exceeding $B_1$ contribute exponent $0$, so
$K(B_1,y)=K(B_1,\min(y,B_1))$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Largest prime factor]
$\Pplus(n):=\max\{p:p\mid n\}$ for $n\ge 2$, with $\Pplus(0)=\Pplus(1)=0$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Firing threshold and normalized index]
An order $n$ \emph{fires at} $y$ if $n\mid K(B_1,y)$, and is \emph{stage-one
reachable} if $n\mid K(B_1)$. The firing threshold is
$\inf\{y:n\mid K(B_1,y)\}$; the normalized firing index is
$\pi(\text{threshold})/\pi(B_1)\in[0,1]$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Late primes and late orders]
$\Late(B_1,y):=\{p \text{ prime}: y<p\le B_1\}$ and
\[
  \Olate(M,B_1,y):=\{n\in(0,M]:\exists\,p\in\Late(B_1,y),\ p\mid n\}.
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:primediv}
Every prime dividing $K(B_1,y)$ is at most $y$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
If the prime $q$ divides $\prod_{p\in\mathcal{P}(y)}p^{\lfloor\log_p
B_1\rfloor}$ then it divides one of the factors $p^{\lfloor\log_p B_1\rfloor}$,
hence divides $p$, hence equals $p$; and $p\le y$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Trace Law]\label{thm:trace}
Let $n\ge 1$ satisfy $n\mid K(B_1)$. Then for every $y\ge 0$,
\[
  n\mid K(B_1,y)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \Pplus(n)\le y .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
($\Rightarrow$) If $n=1$ then $\Pplus(n)=0\le y$. Otherwise
$\Pplus(n)\mid n\mid K(B_1,y)$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:primediv} gives
$\Pplus(n)\le y$.

($\Leftarrow$) Suppose $\Pplus(n)\le y$. Split the full multiplier along the
cut, $K(B_1)=A\cdot B$ with
\[
  A=\prod_{\substack{p\le B_1\\ p\le y}}p^{\lfloor\log_p B_1\rfloor},
  \qquad
  B=\prod_{\substack{p\le B_1\\ p> y}}p^{\lfloor\log_p B_1\rfloor}.
\]
Every prime occurring in $B$ exceeds $y\ge \Pplus(n)$ and hence does not divide
$n$, so $\gcd(n,B)=1$. From $n\mid AB$ and coprimality, $n\mid A$; and $A$
divides $K(B_1,y)$ because its index set is contained in $\mathcal{P}(y)$ with
the same exponents.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Exact threshold]\label{cor:threshold}
For stage-one reachable $n\ge1$, the set $\{y:n\mid K(B_1,y)\}$ has least
element exactly $\Pplus(n)$, and
$\idx(n)=\pi(\Pplus(n))/\pi(B_1)$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[Monotonicity]
If $\Pplus(m)\le \Pplus(n)$ then $\idx(m)\le\idx(n)$: the firing order is the
largest-prime-factor order.
\end{corollary}

\begin{remark}[Work-weighted form]
Since $p^{\lfloor\log_p B_1\rfloor}\le B_1$ for each schedule prime, we have
$K(B_1,y)\le B_1^{\pi(y)}$: an order with a small largest prime factor is
killed by a scalar of small bit length, not merely at an early step index.
Conversely $\prod_{p\le B_1}p$ divides $K(B_1)$, since
$\lfloor\log_p B_1\rfloor\ge 1$ for every $p\le B_1$.
\end{remark}

The trace is thus a \emph{lossy} observable in a precise sense: it records
$\Pplus(n)$ and discards the magnitude of $n$, its number of prime factors, and
its exponent pattern. Every prediction about the firing index is a prediction
about largest prime factors, transported through the compression $\pi$.

\section{The late tail is structurally thin: refutation of H1}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:latelarge}
If $n\mid K(B_1)$ and $n\nmid K(B_1,y)$, there is a prime $p\in\Late(B_1,y)$
with $p\mid n$; indeed $p=\Pplus(n)$ works.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:trace} forces $\Pplus(n)>y$, so $n\ge2$ and $\Pplus(n)$ is a
genuine prime divisor. Applying Theorem~\ref{thm:trace} with $y:=B_1$ gives
$\Pplus(n)\le B_1$. Hence $\Pplus(n)\in(y,B_1]$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Union bound on the late tail]\label{thm:sieve}
For all $M,B_1,y$,
\[
  \#\Olate(M,B_1,y)\;\le\;\sum_{p\in\Late(B_1,y)}\Big\lfloor\frac{M}{p}\Big\rfloor
  \;\le\; M\sum_{p\in\Late(B_1,y)}\frac{1}{p}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$\Olate$ is contained in the union over $p\in\Late(B_1,y)$ of
$\{n\le M: p\mid n\}$, each of cardinality $\lfloor M/p\rfloor$; sub-additivity
gives the first bound, $\lfloor M/p\rfloor\le M/p$ the second.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exactness in the short range]\label{thm:exact}
If $M\le y^{2}$ the union is disjoint and
$\#\Olate(M,B_1,y)=\sum_{p\in\Late(B_1,y)}\lfloor M/p\rfloor$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If distinct late primes $p\ne q$ both divided $n\le M$, coprimality would give
$pq\mid n$, hence $y^{2}<pq\le n\le M\le y^{2}$, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

Thus for $M\le y^{2}$ the late-firing density is \emph{exactly} a truncated
reciprocal prime sum: the trace law converts a positional question about the
algorithm's ladder into a question about $\sum_{y<p\le B_1}1/p$.

\subsection{The concrete instance \texorpdfstring{$B_1=100$}{B1=100}}

Take $B_1=100$, so $\pi(100)=25$, and cut at $y=67$, i.e.\ after step
$\pi(67)=19$. Then $\Late(100,67)=\{71,73,79,83,89,97\}$: the final six steps,
$24\%$ of the schedule by step count, a window at least as generous as the
registered ``final $20\%$''.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:recip}
$\displaystyle\sum_{p\in\Late(100,67)}\frac1p=0.07401\ldots<\frac{2}{25}=0.08 .$
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Refutation of H1 at $B_1=100$]\label{thm:h1}
For every $M\ge1$, $\ \#\Olate(M,100,67)<\tfrac{2}{25}M=0.08\,M$. Uniformity
over the final $24\%$ of the schedule would require density $0.24$; even the
weaker registered target $0.20$ exceeds the structural cap by a factor of
$2.5$. Uniformity of the firing index is impossible, not merely unobserved.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Combine Theorem~\ref{thm:sieve} with Lemma~\ref{lem:recip}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact value and sandwich]
With $M=67^{2}=4489$, Theorem~\ref{thm:exact} applies and
\[
  \#\Olate(4489,100,67)=330,\qquad
  \frac{1}{20}<\frac{330}{4489}=0.07351\ldots<\frac15 .
\]
The late tail is genuinely positive, but carries about one third of the mass
uniformity assigns it.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proposition}[Likelihood of the observed empty tail]\label{prop:lik}
Under the uniform law the probability of an empty final-$20\%$ tail across $55$
independent hits is $(4/5)^{55}=4.677\times10^{-6}$. Under the structural cap
of Theorem~\ref{thm:h1} it is at least $(23/25)^{55}=1.019\times10^{-2}$. Hence
$1000\cdot(4/5)^{55}<(23/25)^{55}$: a likelihood ratio exceeding $2000$ in
favour of the structural law.
\end{proposition}

\section{Asymptotics: the late tail decays like \texorpdfstring{$1/\log B_1$}{1/log B1}}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:primorial}
$\prod_{p\in\Late(B_1,y)}p$ divides the primorial $B_1\#=\prod_{p\le B_1}p$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Chebyshev-type count]\label{thm:cheb}
For $y\ge2$, $\ \#\Late(B_1,y)\cdot\lfloor\log_2 y\rfloor\le 2B_1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write $k=\#\Late(B_1,y)$. Each late prime exceeds $y$, so
$y^{k}\le\prod_{p\in\Late}p$; by Lemma~\ref{lem:primorial} and Erd\H{o}s'
bound $B_1\#\le 4^{B_1}$ that product is at most $4^{B_1}$. Also
$2^{\lfloor\log_2 y\rfloor}\le y$. Chaining,
\[
  2^{k\lfloor\log_2 y\rfloor}=\big(2^{\lfloor\log_2 y\rfloor}\big)^{k}
  \le y^{k}\le\prod_{p\in\Late}p\le 4^{B_1}=2^{2B_1},
\]
and comparing exponents gives the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:sumcard}
$\sum_{p\in\Late(B_1,y)}1/p\le \#\Late(B_1,y)/y$, since each late prime
exceeds $y$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Unconditional late-density bound]\label{thm:density}
For all $M,B_1$ and every cut $y\ge2$,
\[
  \#\Olate(M,B_1,y)\;\le\;\frac{2MB_1}{y\,\lfloor\log_2 y\rfloor}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:sieve}, then Lemma~\ref{lem:sumcard}, then
Theorem~\ref{thm:cheb}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[No constant-fraction late tail]\label{cor:decay}
If $B_1\le 2y$ then
$\#\Olate(M,B_1,y)/M\le 4/\lfloor\log_2 y\rfloor\to0$. In particular no fixed
positive fraction --- such as H1's $20\%$ --- can be the late tail for all
large $B_1$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{example}
At $B_1=2^{20}$ with cut $y=2^{19}$ the late density is below
$4/19\approx0.2105$; at $B_1=2^{26}$, below $0.16$; at $B_1=2^{32}$, below
$0.129$. The bound is deliberately crude, but its direction is unconditional.
\end{example}

\section{Model discrimination: integer model versus divisor model}

The bounds above concern a specific null model: the order is a uniform
\emph{integer} in $(0,M]$. The competing model --- implicit whenever one says
``the accounting is collision-dominated'' --- takes the order to be a uniform
\emph{divisor of $K(B_1)$}. That model is computable exactly, and it predicts
the opposite.

\begin{theorem}[Divisor firing set]\label{thm:divfire}
$\{d\mid K(B_1): \Pplus(d)\le y\}=\{d: d\mid K(B_1,y)\}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Immediate from Theorem~\ref{thm:trace} in both directions, using
$K(B_1,y)\mid K(B_1)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:tau}
For a finite set $S$ of primes and any $e:S\to\mathbb{N}$,
$\tau\big(\prod_{p\in S}p^{e(p)}\big)=\prod_{p\in S}(e(p)+1)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Divisor-model firing law]\label{thm:divlaw}
For all $B_1,y$,
\[
  \tau\big(K(B_1)\big)=\tau\big(K(B_1,y)\big)\cdot
  \prod_{p\in\Late(B_1,y)}\big(\lfloor\log_p B_1\rfloor+1\big),
\]
so a uniformly random divisor of $K(B_1)$ fires by position $y$ with
probability exactly
$\big(\prod_{p\in\Late(B_1,y)}(\lfloor\log_p B_1\rfloor+1)\big)^{-1}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Split $\mathcal{P}(B_1)=\mathcal{P}(\min(y,B_1))\sqcup\Late(B_1,y)$; the two
resulting factors of $K(B_1)$ are coprime, so $\tau$ is multiplicative across
them. Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:tau} to the late factor and
Theorem~\ref{thm:divfire} to identify the early factor with $\tau(K(B_1,y))$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The divisor model fires late]
At $B_1=100$, $y=67$ each late prime has $\lfloor\log_p100\rfloor=1$, so the
local factor is $2^{6}=64$ and $\tau(K(100))=64\,\tau(K(100,67))$; the divisor
model places $63/64=98.44\%$ of its firing mass in the final six schedule
steps. Numerically $\tau(K(100))=660{,}602{,}880$ and
$\tau(K(100,67))=10{,}321{,}920$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Discrimination]
On the measured observable --- mass in the final six of twenty-five schedule
steps at $B_1=100$ --- the integer model caps the mass at $2/25=0.08$ while the
divisor model requires $63/64=0.984$. Since $12\cdot(2/25)<63/64$, the models
differ by more than a factor of twelve and the observable is decisive between
them.
\end{theorem}

\begin{corollary}[Verdict]
The measured empty tail has likelihood $(1/64)^{55}\approx4.6\times10^{-100}$
under the divisor model versus $\ge10^{-2}$ under the integer model. As far as
the firing trace is concerned, the order behaves like a random \emph{integer}
below $B_1$, not like a random \emph{divisor} of the stage-one multiplier: the
early-fire signature is the $\pi$-compression of a typical largest prime factor.
\end{corollary}

\section{The collision baseline: refutation of H2}

\begin{definition}
The \emph{collision probability} of a run of $k$ guarded group operations
modulo $p$ is $\coll(p,k):=1-(1-1/p)^{k}$: the chance that some intermediate
quantity is accidentally divisible by $p$, irrespective of the point's order.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Bernoulli ceiling]\label{thm:bern}
For every prime $p$ and every $k\ge0$, $\coll(p,k)\le k/p$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Bernoulli's inequality $(1+x)^{k}\ge1+kx$ holds for $x\ge-2$; take $x=-1/p$ to
get $(1-1/p)^{k}\ge1-k/p$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Scale freedom]\label{thm:scale}
If $k/p=\ell/q$ then $\coll(p,k)\le\ell/q$ and $\coll(q,\ell)\le k/p$: the
ceiling is a function of the ratio alone.
\end{theorem}

In the experiment $k=c\,B_1$ and the design fixes $B_1/p$, so
$k/p=c\,(B_1/p)$ is invariant across bit lengths by construction. A
collision-dominated account therefore predicts the \emph{same} ceiling at $26$
and $32$ bits. H2 asserted a collapse toward a floor that does not move; the
measured flatness ($65.0\%$ vs.\ $62.5\%$, $z$-test $p=0.8161$) is what both
hypotheses predict and discriminates neither. As posed, H2 was not a test.

What discriminates is the level. The pre-registration used $c=1.44$, giving a
per-curve floor $1-\exp(-1.44\cdot0.125)=16.47\%$. Auditing the implementation
showed the honest count is $c=2.59$; both are reported. With $c=2.59$ and
$B_1/p=0.125$ we get $k/p=0.32375<0.324$, so by Theorem~\ref{thm:bern} the
per-curve collision probability is at most $0.324$ for \emph{every} prime $p$.
(Exponential-model per-curve means are $27.1$--$27.8\%$; three-curve cell means
under exact-operation collision arithmetic are $61.2$--$62.3\%$.)

\begin{theorem}[Subdominance]
If $k\le0.324\,p$ and the observed rate satisfies $\mathrm{obs}\ge0.625$, then
$\coll(p,k)+0.3\le\mathrm{obs}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$\coll(p,k)\le k/p\le0.324$ and $0.324+0.3=0.624\le0.625\le\mathrm{obs}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Pigeonhole]
Let $S$ be the successful curves in a batch and $C$ the collision-driven ones.
Then $\#(S\setminus C)\ge\#S-\#C$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$S\subseteq(S\setminus C)\cup C$, so $\#S\le\#(S\setminus C)+\#C$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The measured cell]
In a cell of $40$ curves with $25$ successes, at most
$\lfloor0.324\cdot40\rfloor=12$ can be collision-driven, so at least $13$
successes are genuine order-hits.
\end{corollary}

Collisions are real and non-negligible --- up to a third of per-curve successes
at the operating point --- but they are subdominant, and the collision
hypothesis is structurally incapable of predicting the cross-scale collapse H2
asserted.

\section{Computation}

We report direct computation over uniform orders, taking $B_1=N$ and letting
$n$ range over all integers in $(0,N]$, with the firing index
$\pi(\Pplus(n))/\pi(N)$ evaluated by a largest-prime-factor sieve at cost
$O(N\log\log N)$.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{rrrrrr}
\toprule
$N$ & $\pi(N)$ & median & mean & final $20\%$ & first $20\%$\\
\midrule
$10^{3}$ & $168$   & $0.083$ & $0.176$ & $3.4\%$ & $73.0\%$\\
$10^{4}$ & $1229$  & $0.035$ & $0.122$ & $2.5\%$ & $81.7\%$\\
$10^{5}$ & $9592$  & $0.014$ & $0.091$ & $1.9\%$ & $86.3\%$\\

A uniform firing index would produce $0.500$ in the median and mean columns and

final-$20\%$ mass decays monotonically in line with Corollary~\ref{cor:decay},
and the first-$20\%$ mass rises toward $90\%$. Direct verification of the trace
law on all (divisor, cut) pairs for $B_1\in\{12,20,30\}$ --- $576$, $8640$ and
$84{,}480$ pairs --- records zero violations.

\section{Discussion}

\subsection{Why the intuition failed}

H1 rested on the picture that ``order completion takes the whole schedule''.
It is wrong for a specific reason: by the time the walk has passed a prime $p$,
the accumulated scalar already contains $p$ to the \emph{maximum} exponent
stage one will ever supply. A reachable order is therefore satisfied the
instant its largest prime factor has been passed --- and largest prime factors
of typical integers are small. The $\pi$-rescaling amplifies this, because
prime density falls off: moving from step $\pi(y)$ to $\pi(2y)$ costs many
schedule steps but adds only sparse, high primes that few orders need.

\subsection{The trace law as a bridge}

Theorem~\ref{thm:trace} says the firing trace is an observable of $\Pplus$, so
classical results on the distribution of the largest prime factor become
predictions about the algorithm's runtime profile, and conversely a measured
trace probes $\Pplus$ statistics on the arithmetically constrained population
of elliptic-curve group orders. The Dickman function $\rho$, governing
$\Pr[\Pplus(n)\le n^{1/u}]\to\rho(u)$, and Golomb's results on largest-prime-factor
distributions, are the natural asymptotic inputs;
Theorem~\ref{thm:exact} shows the finite-range problem is exactly a truncated
Mertens sum.

\subsection{Honest caveats}

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Operation-count constant.} The registered baseline used
$c=1.44$; the honest count is $c=2.59$. All baselines are recomputed both ways
and both reported. The corrected floor weakens --- but does not overturn ---
the excess argument.
\item \textbf{Numerical coincidence.} Under exact-operation collision
arithmetic, three-curve cell means are $61.2$--$62.3\%$, close to the measured
cell rates. This is flagged rather than suppressed: the per-curve excess, the
trace-shape rejection, and the empty late tail are what rule out collision
dominance; the cell-level rate alone would not.
\item \textbf{Censoring.} Successes attributable purely to the second cofactor
are censored from the accounting and not counted as order-hits, a conservative
choice.
\item \textbf{Silent failure mode.} One class of degenerate curves collapses
without a diagnostic; this behaviour is inherited from the parent design.
\item \textbf{Bound crudeness.} Corollary~\ref{cor:decay} discards prime
sparsity beyond the Erd\H{o}s estimate; the true decay is expected to follow
the Mertens law below.
\item \textbf{Independence.} Proposition~\ref{prop:lik} treats the $55$ hits as
independent Bernoulli trials, as the registered binomial test did;
correlations would inflate both likelihoods but not, to first order, their
ratio.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{A caught error, reported}

During instrumentation the closed-form step counter used to cross-check the
traced counter was initially wrong on later chunks of the schedule: the
relevant length \emph{doubles} and the population count \emph{adds}, rather
than the off-by-one behaviour first coded. The discrepancy was caught by an
assertion comparing traced against closed-form counts before any full dataset
existed, fixed, and re-verified against $29$ of $29$ smoke curves; smoke data
were regenerated after the fix. No result here depends on the pre-fix counter.

\subsection{Where this sits}

This is an audit that closes an evidence chain rather than a breach of any
barrier. An earlier finding --- that no abrupt destruction threshold appears in
the regime studied --- was challenged on the grounds that its accounting
conflated smoothness hits with collisions. The proposed amendment is rejected
here on two independent grounds (level and trace shape), and the earlier
no-threshold account stands unamended. No constant is improved and no
complexity claim is made. What is new is the trace law and the family of bounds
it generates.

\section{Future work}

\subsection{The Mertens Firing-Tail Law}

Cut the schedule at the $(1-\tau)$-quantile, i.e.\ at $y$ with
$\pi(y)=(1-\tau)\pi(B_1)$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:exact} the late-firing density
in the short range is $\sum_{y<p\le B_1}1/p$, which Mertens' second theorem
evaluates as $\log\log B_1-\log\log y+o(1)$.

\begin{conjecture}[Mertens Firing-Tail Law]
\[
  \mathrm{tail}(\tau,B_1)=\frac{\log\big(1/(1-\tau)\big)}{\log B_1}\big(1+o(1)\big)
  \qquad (B_1\to\infty).
\]
\end{conjecture}

At $\tau=0.2$ the numerator is $\log(1.25)=0.2231$, and the prediction against
the computed table is:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{rrr}
\toprule
$B_1$ & predicted $\mathrm{tail}(0.2)$ & measured\\
\midrule
$10^{3}$ & $0.0323$ & $0.0340$\\
$10^{4}$ & $0.0242$ & $0.0250$\\
$10^{5}$ & $0.0194$ & $0.0190$\\
$10^{6}$ & $0.0162$ & $0.0160$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Proving the conjecture requires an effective form of Mertens' theorem over the
truncated range, control of the $\pi$-quantile-to-value conversion, and an
inclusion--exclusion correction beyond the short range $M\le y^{2}$.

\subsection{Further directions}

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Beyond the short range.} A second-order term
$-\sum_{y<p<q\le B_1}\lfloor M/pq\rfloor$ should extend exactness to
$M\le y^{3}$, with a full Legendre-type expansion giving the tail to all orders.
\item \textbf{Sharper Chebyshev input.} Replacing $4^{B_1}$ by an effective
bound $\theta(x)<1.001102\,x$ would improve the constant in
Theorem~\ref{thm:density} from $2$ to roughly $1.45/\log 2$.
\item \textbf{Stage two.} The continuation phase admits a single extra large
prime; the trace law should extend to a two-parameter statement with the late
tail governed by a two-dimensional Dickman-type region.
\item \textbf{Order-population bias.} Elliptic-curve group orders are biased by
torsion structure; quantifying the deviation of $\Pplus$ statistics from the
uniform-integer baseline would sharpen every density estimate here.
\item \textbf{Early-abort scheduling.} If nine-tenths of the firing mass lies
in the first fifth of the schedule, a fractional stage-one run captures most of
the hits of a full run; allocating a fixed operation budget across curves and
schedule fractions becomes a tractable optimization problem.
\item \textbf{Trace as a diagnostic.} Since the firing index reads off
$\pi(\Pplus(n))/\pi(B_1)$, an observed trace directly measures the largest
prime factor of the hidden group order, usable to re-tune $B_1$ adaptively.
\end{itemize}

\section{Conclusion}

The moment at which stage one of the elliptic-curve method succeeds is not a
complicated function of the run: it is the largest prime factor of the point's
order, read through the prime-counting function. From that single identity
follow the structural thinness of the late tail (below $8\%$ at $B_1=100$
versus $20$--$24\%$ under uniformity), its unconditional decay like $1/\log$,
the exact firing law of the competing divisor model and its refutation by more
than a factor of twelve, and --- on the rate side --- the scale freedom of the
collision baseline together with a level gap of thirty percentage points that
pigeonholes into at least thirteen genuine order-hits per measured cell.

Two pre-registered hypotheses died. The replacement is not another statistical
claim but a theorem, and it points at one of the oldest questions in
multiplicative number theory: how big is the biggest prime in a random integer?
Almost always, small --- which is precisely why this clock always strikes early.

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Dict, Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Elementary sieves
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def primes_up_to(n: int) -> List[int]:
    """All primes p <= n, by a simple sieve of Eratosthenes.  O(n log log n)."""
    if n < 2:
        return []
    sieve = bytearray([1]) * (n + 1)
    sieve[0] = sieve[1] = 0
    for p in range(2, int(n**0.5) + 1):
        if sieve[p]:
            sieve[p * p :: p] = bytearray(len(sieve[p * p :: p]))
    return [i for i in range(n + 1) if sieve[i]]


def largest_prime_factor_table(n: int) -> List[int]:
    """largest_prime_factor_table(n)[m] = P+(m), the largest prime factor of m.

    Entries for m = 0 and m = 1 are 0 by convention.  Computed by sweeping each
    prime p over its multiples, so the last prime written for m is the largest.
    Cost O(n log log n) time, O(n) memory.
    """
    lpf = [0] * (n + 1)
    for p in range(2, n + 1):
        if lpf[p] == 0:  # p is prime
            for multiple in range(p, n + 1, p):
                lpf[multiple] = p
    return lpf


def prime_counting(n: int, primes: Sequence[int]) -> int:
    """pi(n), given a sorted list of primes covering [0, n]."""
    lo, hi = 0, len(primes)
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if primes[mid] <= n:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid
    return lo


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. The stage-one schedule
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def stage_product(b1: int, y: int) -> int:
    """K(B1, y) = prod_{p <= y} p^{floor(log_p B1)}: the accumulated scalar
    after the stage-one schedule has consumed every prime up to y."""
    result = 1
    for p in primes_up_to(min(y, b1)):
        exponent = int(math.log(b1) / math.log(p) + 1e-12)
        result *= p**exponent
    return result


def max_prime_factor(n: int) -> int:
    """P+(n) by trial division; 0 for n in {0, 1}."""
    if n <= 1:
        return 0
    best, m, d = 1, n, 2
    while d * d <= m:
        while m % d == 0:
            best, m = d, m // d
        d += 1
    return max(best, m)


def stage_exponents(b1: int, y: int) -> Dict[int, int]:
    """The exponent vector of K(B1, y): p -> floor(log_p B1) for each p <= y."""
    return {p: int(math.log(b1) / math.log(p) + 1e-12)
            for p in primes_up_to(min(y, b1))}


def divisor_count(exponents: Dict[int, int]) -> int:
    """tau of a number given as a prime-exponent vector: prod (e_p + 1)."""
    total = 1
    for exponent in exponents.values():
        total *= exponent + 1
    return total


def divisors_with_max_prime(exponents: Dict[int, int]) -> Iterable[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """Enumerate every divisor of the number with the given prime-exponent
    vector, together with its largest prime factor (0 for the divisor 1).
    Enumerating from the exponent vector avoids any factorization work."""
    items: List[Tuple[int, int]] = sorted(exponents.items())

    def walk(index: int, value: int, mpf: int) -> Iterable[Tuple[int, int]]:
        if index == len(items):
            yield value, mpf
            return
        p, e = items[index]
        power = 1
        for exponent in range(e + 1):
            yield from walk(index + 1, value * power,
                            p if exponent > 0 else mpf)
            power *= p

    return walk(0, 1, 0)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Demonstration blocks
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def verify_trace_law(b1: int = 30) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Check `n | K(B1,y) <==> P+(n) <= y` on every divisor n of K(B1,B1) and
    every schedule cut y.  Returns (checks_done, failures)."""
    cuts: List[int] = [0] + primes_up_to(b1)
    partial: Dict[int, int] = {y: stage_product(b1, y) for y in cuts}
    checks = 0
    failures = 0
    for n, mpf in divisors_with_max_prime(stage_exponents(b1, b1)):
        for y in cuts:
            lhs = partial[y] % n == 0
            rhs = mpf <= y
            checks += 1
            if lhs != rhs:
                failures += 1
    return checks, failures


def firing_index_statistics(n_max: int) -> Dict[str, float]:
    """Empirical distribution of the normalized firing index
    pi(P+(n)) / pi(N) for n uniform in (0, N], with the stage-one bound
    B1 = N.  Returns median, mean, final-20% tail mass and first-20% mass."""
    primes = primes_up_to(n_max)
    lpf = largest_prime_factor_table(n_max)
    total_steps = len(primes)
    # rank[p] = pi(p) for prime p; built once
    rank: Dict[int, int] = {p: i + 1 for i, p in enumerate(primes)}
    indices: List[float] = []
    for n in range(2, n_max + 1):
        indices.append(rank[lpf[n]] / total_steps)
    indices.sort()
    count = len(indices)
    median = indices[count // 2]
    mean = sum(indices) / count
    tail = sum(1 for x in indices if x > 0.8) / count
    head = sum(1 for x in indices if x <= 0.2) / count
    return {
        "N": float(n_max),
        "steps": float(total_steps),
        "median": median,
        "mean": mean,
        "final_20pct_mass": tail,
        "first_20pct_mass": head,
    }


def exact_late_tail(m: int, b1: int, y: int) -> int:
    """Exact number of integers n in (0, M] whose firing position exceeds y,
    i.e. that are divisible by some prime in (y, B1].  For M <= y^2 no integer
    can carry two such primes, so this equals sum_{y < p <= B1} floor(M/p)."""
    late_primes = [p for p in primes_up_to(b1) if p > y]
    return sum(m // p for p in late_primes)


def divisor_model_late_factor(b1: int, y: int) -> int:
    """prod_{y < p <= B1} (floor(log_p B1) + 1): the exact factor by which the
    divisor count of the full stage-one multiplier exceeds that of the partial
    product at cut y.  The divisor model therefore fires *late* with
    probability 1 - 1/factor."""
    factor = 1
    for p in primes_up_to(b1):
        if p > y:
            factor *= int(math.log(b1) / math.log(p) + 1e-12) + 1
    return factor


def collision_probability(p: int, k: int) -> float:
    """1 - (1 - 1/p)^k: the chance that k guarded group operations modulo p
    accidentally hit a multiple of p, independently of the point's order.
    Evaluated as -expm1(k * log1p(-1/p)) so it stays accurate for huge p."""
    return -math.expm1(k * math.log1p(-1.0 / p))


def late_density_log_bound(b1: int, y: int) -> float:
    """The unconditional structural cap 2*B1 / (y * floor(log2 y)) on the
    fraction of orders that can fire after schedule position y."""
    return 2.0 * b1 / (y * math.floor(math.log2(y)))

    for n in range(2, n_max + 1):
        indices.append(rank[lpf[n]] / total_steps)
    indices.sort()
    count = len(indices)
    median = indices[count // 2]
    mean = sum(indices) / count
    tail = sum(1 for x in indices if x > 0.8) / count
    head = sum(1 for x in indices if x <= 0.2) / count
    return {
        "N": float(n_max),
        "steps": float(total_steps),
        "median": median,
        "mean": mean,
        "final_20pct_mass": tail,
        "first_20pct_mass": head,
    }


def exact_late_tail(m: int, b1: int, y: int) -> int:
    """Exact number of integers n in (0, M] whose firing position exceeds y,
    i.e. that are divisible by some prime in (y, B1].  For M <= y^2 no integer
    can carry two such primes, so this equals sum_{y < p <= B1} floor(M/p)."""
    late_primes = [p for p in primes_up_to(b1) if p > y]
    return sum(m // p for p in late_primes)


def divisor_model_late_factor(b1: int, y: int) -> int:
    """prod_{y < p <= B1} (floor(log_p B1) + 1): the exact factor by which the
    divisor count of the full stage-one multiplier exceeds that of the partial
    product at cut y.  The divisor model therefore fires *late* with
    probability 1 - 1/factor."""
    factor = 1
    for p in primes_up_to(b1):
        if p > y:
            factor *= int(math.log(b1) / math.log(p) + 1e-12) + 1
    return factor


def collision_probability(p: int, k: int) -> float:
    """1 - (1 - 1/p)^k: the chance that k guarded group operations modulo p
    accidentally hit a multiple of p, independently of the point's order.
    Evaluated as -expm1(k * log1p(-1/p)) so it stays accurate for huge p."""
    return -math.expm1(k * math.log1p(-1.0 / p))


def late_density_log_bound(b1: int, y: int) -> float:
    """The unconditional structural cap 2*B1 / (y * floor(log2 y)) on the
    fraction of orders that can fire after schedule position y."""
    return 2.0 * b1 / (y * math.floor(math.log2(y)))

def sieve_largest_prime_factor(n: int) -> List[int]:
    """lpf[m] = largest prime factor of m, for 0 <= m <= n (0 for m < 2)."""
    lpf: List[int] = [0] * (n + 1)
    for p in range(2, n + 1):
        if lpf[p] == 0:
            for multiple in range(p, n + 1, p):
                lpf[multiple] = p
    return lpf


def prime_ranks(n: int, lpf: Sequence[int]) -> Dict[int, int]:
    """rank[p] = pi(p) for every prime p <= n, read off the sieve."""
    rank: Dict[int, int] = {}
    counter = 0
    for m in range(2, n + 1):
        if lpf[m] == m:  # m is prime
            counter += 1
            rank[m] = counter
    return rank


def firing_indices(n_max: int) -> List[float]:
    """The multiset { pi(P+(n)) / pi(N) : 2 <= n <= N }, sorted ascending."""
    lpf = sieve_largest_prime_factor(n_max)
    rank = prime_ranks(n_max, lpf)
    total = max(rank.values())
    values = [rank[lpf[n]] / total for n in range(2, n_max + 1)]
    values.sort()
    return values


def quantile(sorted_values: Sequence[float], q: float) -> float:
    """The q-quantile of an already-sorted sequence."""
    if not sorted_values:
        return float("nan")
    position = min(len(sorted_values) - 1, int(q * len(sorted_values)))
    return sorted_values[position]


def histogram(values: Sequence[float], bins: int = 20) -> List[float]:
    """Relative mass of `values` in each of `bins` equal bins of [0, 1]."""
    counts = [0] * bins
    for value in values:
        index = min(bins - 1, int(value * bins))
        counts[index] += 1
    total = len(values)
    return [c / total for c in counts]


def mertens_tail_prediction(tau: float, b1: int) -> float:
    """Conjectured late-tail mass log(1/(1-tau)) / log(B1)."""
    return math.log(1.0 / (1.0 - tau)) / math.log(b1)


def structural_cap(b1: int, y: int) -> float:
    """The unconditional cap 2*B1 / (y * floor(log2 y)) on the late-tail
    density, valid for every cut y >= 2."""
    return 2.0 * b1 / (y * math.floor(math.log2(y)))

from typing import Dict, List, Optional, Sequence, Tuple


def sieve_primes(limit: int) -> List[int]:
    """All primes <= limit by the sieve of Eratosthenes.  O(limit log log limit)."""
    if limit < 2:
        return []
    flags = bytearray([1]) * (limit + 1)
    flags[0] = flags[1] = 0
    for p in range(2, int(limit**0.5) + 1):
        if flags[p]:
            flags[p * p :: p] = bytearray(len(flags[p * p :: p]))
    return [i for i, f in enumerate(flags) if f]


def largest_prime_factor(n: int, primes: Sequence[int]) -> int:
    """P+(n), using a precomputed prime list that covers sqrt(n).
    Returns 0 for n in {0, 1}.  Cost O(pi(sqrt(n)))."""
    if n <= 1:
        return 0
    best = 1
    remaining = n
    for p in primes:
        if p * p > remaining:
            break
        while remaining % p == 0:
            best = p
            remaining //= p
    return max(best, remaining)


def firing_threshold(order: int, b1: int) -> Optional[int]:
    """The exact schedule position at which a stage-one run with bound `b1`
    annihilates a point of the given `order`.

    By the trace law the threshold equals P+(order), provided the order is
    stage-one reachable.  Reachability is checked without ever forming the
    astronomically large multiplier K(B1): the order is reachable exactly when
    every prime power p^e exactly dividing it satisfies p <= B1 and
    e <= floor(log_p B1).  Returns None when the order is unreachable, i.e.
    when the run never fires.

    Complexity: O(sqrt(order) / log(order)) for the factorization, O(1) after.
    """
    if order <= 0:
        return None
    if order == 1:
        return 0
    primes = sieve_primes(int(order**0.5) + 1)
    remaining = order
    max_prime = 1
    for p in primes:
        if p * p > remaining:
            break
        if remaining % p == 0:
            exponent = 0
            while remaining % p == 0:
                remaining //= p
                exponent += 1
            budget = 0
            power = p
            while power <= b1:
                budget += 1
                power *= p
            if p > b1 or exponent > budget:
                return None
            max_prime = max(max_prime, p)
    if remaining > 1:
        if remaining > b1:
            return None
        max_prime = max(max_prime, remaining)
    return max_prime


def normalized_firing_index(order: int, b1: int) -> Optional[float]:
    """pi(P+(order)) / pi(B1): the position of the hit as a fraction of the
    stage-one schedule.  None when the order is not stage-one reachable."""
    threshold = firing_threshold(order, b1)
    if threshold is None:
        return None
    schedule = sieve_primes(b1)
    if not schedule:
        return None
    consumed = sum(1 for p in schedule if p <= threshold)
    return consumed / len(schedule)

import math

def sieve_primes(limit: int) -> List[int]:
    """All primes <= limit.  O(limit log log limit)."""
    if limit < 2:
        return []
    flags = bytearray([1]) * (limit + 1)
    flags[0] = flags[1] = 0

        if flags[p]:
            flags[p * p :: p] = bytearray(len(flags[p * p :: p]))
    return [i for i, f in enumerate(flags) if f]


def late_primes(b1: int, cut: int) -> List[int]:
    """The schedule primes strictly beyond the cut: { p prime : cut < p <= B1 }."""
    return [p for p in sieve_primes(b1) if p > cut]


def late_count_union_bound(m: int, b1: int, cut: int) -> int:
    """Union bound on the number of orders in (0, M] that fire after `cut`:
    sum over late primes p of floor(M / p).  Always an upper bound; exact
    whenever M <= cut^2, because then no order can carry two late primes."""
    return sum(m // p for p in late_primes(b1, cut))


def late_count_exact(m: int, b1: int, cut: int) -> int:
    """Exact count of orders in (0, M] divisible by at least one late prime,
    by inclusion-exclusion over the late primes (feasible when the number of
    late primes is modest).  Complexity O(2^k) with k = #late primes; for
    M <= cut^2 the union bound already coincides with this value."""
    late = late_primes(b1, cut)
    if m <= cut * cut:
        return late_count_union_bound(m, b1, cut)
    total = 0
    count = len(late)
    for mask in range(1, 1 << count):
        product = 1
        bits = 0
        for index in range(count):
            if mask >> index & 1:
                product *= late[index]
                bits += 1
                if product > m:
                    break
        if product <= m:
            total += (m // product) if bits % 2 == 1 else -(m // product)
    return total


def reciprocal_cap(b1: int, cut: int) -> float:
    """sum_{cut < p <= B1} 1/p : the limiting density of late firers."""
    return sum(1.0 / p for p in late_primes(b1, cut))


def primorial_cap(b1: int, cut: int) -> float:
    """The unconditional cap 2*B1 / (cut * floor(log2 cut)) derived from
    Erdos' primorial bound prod_{p <= x} p <= 4^x, valid for cut >= 2 and
    requiring no prime enumeration at all: O(1)."""
    if cut < 2:
        return float("inf")
    return 2.0 * b1 / (cut * math.floor(math.log2(cut)))


def late_tail_report(m: int, b1: int, cut: int) -> Dict[str, float]:
    """Assemble every bound and the exact value for one (M, B1, cut) triple."""
    exact = late_count_exact(m, b1, cut)

        "exact_density": exact / m,
        "union_bound_density": late_count_union_bound(m, b1, cut) / m,
        "reciprocal_cap": reciprocal_cap(b1, cut),
        "primorial_cap": primorial_cap(b1, cut),
        "uniform_claim": (
            len(late_primes(b1, cut)) / max(1, len(sieve_primes(b1)))

    }

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple


def sieve_primes(limit: int) -> List[int]:
    """All primes <= limit.  O(limit log log limit)."""
    if limit < 2:
        return []
    flags = bytearray([1]) * (limit + 1)
    flags[0] = flags[1] = 0
    for p in range(2, int(limit**0.5) + 1):
        if flags[p]:
            flags[p * p :: p] = bytearray(len(flags[p * p :: p]))
    return [i for i, f in enumerate(flags) if f]


def stage_exponent(p: int, b1: int) -> int:
    """floor(log_p B1): the exponent stage one gives to the schedule prime p."""
    exponent, power = 0, p
    while power <= b1:
        exponent += 1
        power *= p
    return exponent


def divisor_count_full(b1: int) -> int:
    """tau(K(B1)) = prod_{p <= B1} (floor(log_p B1) + 1), computed from the
    exponent vector, never forming K(B1) itself."""
    total = 1
    for p in sieve_primes(b1):
        total *= stage_exponent(p, b1) + 1
    return total


def divisor_model_late_mass(b1: int, cut: int) -> float:
    """Under the divisor null model the probability of firing by `cut` is the
    reciprocal of prod_{cut < p <= B1} (floor(log_p B1) + 1); the late mass is
    one minus that.  Complexity O(pi(B1))."""
    factor = 1
    for p in sieve_primes(b1):
        if p > cut:
            factor *= stage_exponent(p, b1) + 1
    return 1.0 - 1.0 / factor


def integer_model_late_mass(b1: int, cut: int) -> float:
    """Under the integer null model the late mass is at most the reciprocal
    sum of the late primes (an equality in the short range M <= cut^2)."""
    return sum(1.0 / p for p in sieve_primes(b1) if p > cut)


def uniform_model_late_mass(b1: int, cut: int) -> float:
    """Under the pre-registered uniform law the late mass is simply the
    fraction of schedule steps beyond the cut."""
    primes = sieve_primes(b1)
    return sum(1 for p in primes if p > cut) / len(primes)


def empty_tail_likelihood(mass: float, hits: int) -> float:
    """Probability of observing NO hit in a window carrying probability `mass`
    across `hits` independent successes."""
    return (1.0 - mass) ** hits


def discriminate(b1: int, cut: int, hits: int) -> Dict[str, float]:
    """Full model-discrimination report for an observed empty late tail."""
    masses = {
        "divisor": divisor_model_late_mass(b1, cut),
        "integer": integer_model_late_mass(b1, cut),
        "uniform": uniform_model_late_mass(b1, cut),
    }
    likelihoods = {
        name: empty_tail_likelihood(mass, hits) for name, mass in masses.items()
    }
    best = max(likelihoods, key=lambda name: likelihoods[name])
    report: Dict[str, float] = {}
    for name in masses:
        report[f"mass_{name}"] = masses[name]
        report[f"likelihood_{name}"] = likelihoods[name]
    report["log10_ratio_integer_over_uniform"] = math.log10(
        likelihoods["integer"] / likelihoods["uniform"]
    )
    report["log10_ratio_integer_over_divisor"] = math.log10(
        likelihoods["integer"] / max(likelihoods["divisor"], 1e-300)
    )
    print(f"  selected model: {best}")
    return report


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for key, value in discriminate(b1=100, cut=67, hits=55).items():
        print(f"  {key:>36} : {value:.6g}")

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Dict, Tuple


def collision_probability(p: int, operations: int) -> float:
    """1 - (1 - 1/p)^k, the chance that a run of `operations` guarded group
    operations modulo p accidentally hits a multiple of p.  Evaluated through
    expm1/log1p so it remains accurate for cryptographic-size p.  O(1)."""
    return -math.expm1(operations * math.log1p(-1.0 / p))


def bernoulli_ceiling(p: int, operations: int) -> float:
    """The Bernoulli bound k/p on the collision probability.  Depends only on
    the ratio k/p, hence is invariant under rescaling p at fixed ratio."""
    return operations / p


def operating_point(ratio_b1_over_p: float, ops_per_b1: float) -> float:
    """k/p = ops_per_b1 * (B1/p): the only quantity the collision ceiling
    depends on.  This is why a bit-length sweep at fixed B1/p cannot move the
    ceiling, and therefore cannot test a collision-dominance hypothesis."""
    return ops_per_b1 * ratio_b1_over_p


def order_hit_lower_bound(curves: int, successes: int, ceiling: float) -> int:
    """Pigeonhole: with at most floor(ceiling * curves) collision-driven
    successes, at least successes - floor(ceiling * curves) hits must be
    genuine order-hits.  Never returns a negative number."""
    max_collisions = math.floor(ceiling * curves)
    return max(0, successes - max_collisions)


def audit(
    bit_lengths: Tuple[int, ...] = (26, 32, 48, 64),
    ratio_b1_over_p: float = 0.125,
    ops_per_b1: float = 2.59,
    curves: int = 40,
    successes: int = 25,
) -> Dict[str, float]:
    """Run the full audit: exhibit scale freedom across bit lengths, evaluate
    the ceiling at the operating point, and pigeonhole the order-hit count."""
    ceiling = operating_point(ratio_b1_over_p, ops_per_b1)
    print(f"  operating point k/p = {ops_per_b1} * {ratio_b1_over_p} = {ceiling:.5f}")
    print(f"  {'bits':>6} {'p':>22} {'k':>24} {'coll(p,k)':>11} {'k/p':>9}")
    for bits in bit_lengths:
        p = 2 ** (bits - 1) + 1
        b1 = int(ratio_b1_over_p * p)
        k = int(ops_per_b1 * b1)
        print(f"  {bits:>6} {p:>22} {k:>24} "
              f"{collision_probability(p, k):>11.5f} {bernoulli_ceiling(p, k):>9.5f}")
    hits = order_hit_lower_bound(curves, successes, ceiling)
    print(f"  cell of {curves} curves with {successes} successes: at least "
          f"{hits} genuine order-hits")
    return {
        "ceiling": ceiling,
        "registered_floor_1_44": -math.expm1(-1.44 * ratio_b1_over_p),
        "corrected_floor_2_59": -math.expm1(-ops_per_b1 * ratio_b1_over_p),
        "order_hit_lower_bound": float(hits),
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for key, value in audit().items():
        print(f"  {key:>24} : {value:.6f}")

    --bg:#f7fafc; --accent:#2b6cb0; --good:#2f855a; --bad:#9b2c2c; --warn:#975a16;
  }
  *{box-sizing:border-box}
  body{
    margin:0; padding:24px; background:var(--bg); color:var(--ink);
    font-family:-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,"Segoe UI",Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif;

  }

  h1{font-size:1.6rem;margin:0 0 4px}
  h2{font-size:1.05rem;margin:26px 0 8px;color:var(--muted);
     text-transform:uppercase;letter-spacing:.07em}
  .sub{color:var(--muted);margin:0 0 20px}
  .panel{background:var(--panel);border:1px solid var(--line);border-radius:12px;
         padding:18px 20px;margin-bottom:18px;box-shadow:0 1px 3px rgba(0,0,0,.05)}
  .controls{display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fit,minmax(240px,1fr));gap:18px}
  label{display:block;font-weight:600;font-size:.88rem;margin-bottom:6px}
  input[type=range]{width:100%}
  .val{font-family:ui-monospace,SFMono-Regular,Menlo,monospace;color:var(--accent)}

  th:first-child,td:first-child{text-align:left}

  .verdict{font-size:1.02rem;padding:14px 16px;border-radius:10px;
           background:#f0fff4;border:1px solid #9ae6b4;color:#22543d}
  .verdict.bad{background:#fff5f5;border-color:#feb2b2;color:#742a2a}

       font-family:ui-monospace,SFMono-Regular,Menlo,monospace;font-size:.9em}

  .swatch{display:inline-block;width:12px;height:12px;border-radius:3px;
          margin-right:5px;vertical-align:-1px}

          background:#fbfdff}
