<body>
<div class="wrap">

  <h1>The Firing Trace Explorer</h1>
  <p class="sub">
    Stage one of the elliptic-curve method walks the primes
    <code>p ≤ B₁</code> in increasing order, multiplying an accumulating
    scalar by <code>p^⌊log_p B₁⌋</code> at each step. A point
    of order <em>n</em> dies at the first step where the accumulated scalar is a
    multiple of <em>n</em> — and by the <strong>trace law</strong> that
    happens exactly when the schedule has passed <code>P⁺(n)</code>, the
    largest prime factor of <em>n</em>. Move the sliders and watch where the
    firing mass actually lives.
  </p>

  <div class="panel controls">
    <div>
      <label for="b1">Stage-one bound  B₁ = <span class="val" id="b1v">1000</span>
         (π(B₁) = <span class="val" id="stepsv">168</span> steps)</label>
      <input type="range" id="b1" min="50" max="20000" step="50" value="1000">
    </div>
    <div>
      <label for="cut">Schedule cut  — last <span class="val" id="cutv">20</span>% of the steps
         (y = <span class="val" id="yv">?</span>)</label>
      <input type="range" id="cut" min="2" max="60" step="1" value="20">
    </div>
    <div>
      <label for="hits">Recorded hits in the experiment: <span class="val" id="hitsv">55</span></label>
      <input type="range" id="hits" min="5" max="200" step="1" value="55">
    </div>
  </div>

  <h2>Where the firing mass lives</h2>
  <div class="panel">
    <canvas id="hist" width="1020" height="300"></canvas>
    <p class="legend">
      <span><i class="swatch" style="background:#2b6cb0"></i>measured mass per schedule bin (integer orders)</span>
      <span><i class="swatch" style="background:#a0aec0"></i>uniform law (pre-registered)</span>
      <span><i class="swatch" style="background:#fed7d7"></i>the late window you selected</span>
    </p>
  </div>

  <h2>The three competing accounts</h2>
  <div class="panel">
    <table>
      <thead>
        <tr><th>Account of the firing trace</th><th>Late-window mass</th>
            <th>Likelihood of an empty tail</th><th>Verdict</th></tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody id="models"></tbody>
    </table>
    <p id="verdict" class="verdict"></p>
    <details>
      <summary>Why the divisor model fires late — click for the exact computation</summary>
      <p>
        If the order were a uniformly random <em>divisor</em> of the full stage-one
        multiplier, the trace law would still apply: the divisors that fire by the
        cut <em>y</em> are exactly the divisors of the partial product. Counting
        divisors gives the exact splitting
        <code>τ(K(B₁)) = τ(K(B₁,y)) · ∏<sub>y<p≤B₁</sub> (⌊log_p B₁⌋+1)</code>.
        Each late prime multiplies the divisor count by at least two, so with
        <span id="latecount">?</span> late primes the early-firing probability is
        only <code>1/<span id="latefactor">?</span></code> — the divisor
        model puts nearly all of its mass in the window the integer model caps at
        a few percent. Two natural priors on the order, opposite predictions,
        one decisive measurement.
      </p>
    </details>
    <details>
      <summary>Why the integer model's late tail is thin — the sieve bound</summary>
      <p>
        Firing after the cut forces the order to be divisible by a prime in
        <code>(y, B₁]</code>. Counting the multiples of each such prime below
        <em>M</em> and adding gives the union bound
        <code>#{late firers} ≤ ∑<sub>y<p≤B₁</sub> ⌊M/p⌋</code>,
        so the late density is at most the reciprocal sum
        <code>∑<sub>y<p≤B₁</sub> 1/p</code>. Large primes are sparse and
        their reciprocals are tiny, so this is small — and in the range
        <code>M ≤ y²</code> no order can carry two late primes, which makes
        the bound an exact equality.
      </p>
    </details>
  </div>

  <h2>The schedule, step by step</h2>
  <div class="panel">
    <canvas id="cdf" width="1020" height="260"></canvas>
    <p class="legend">
      <span><i class="swatch" style="background:#2f855a"></i>cumulative firing mass (integer model)</span>
      <span><i class="swatch" style="background:#a0aec0"></i>uniform law diagonal</span>
      <span><i class="swatch" style="background:#dd6b20"></i>median firing index</span>
    </p>
    <p id="summary" style="color:var(--muted);margin-top:10px"></p>
  </div>

</div>

<script>
"use strict";

function sievePrimes(limit){
  const flags = new Uint8Array(limit+1).fill(1);
  flags[0]=0; if(limit>=1) flags[1]=0;
  for(let p=2;p*p<=limit;p++) if(flags[p]) for(let m=p*p;m<=limit;m+=p) flags[m]=0;
  const out=[];
  for(let i=2;i<=limit;i++) if(flags[i]) out.push(i);
  return out;
}

// lpf[m] = largest prime factor of m
function sieveLargestPrimeFactor(limit){
  const lpf = new Int32Array(limit+1);
  for(let p=2;p<=limit;p++){
    if(lpf[p]===0){ for(let m=p;m<=limit;m+=p) lpf[m]=p; }
  }
  return lpf;
}

function stageExponent(p,b1){ let e=0,q=p; while(q<=b1){e++; q*=p;} return e; }

const state = {};

function recompute(){
  const b1  = +document.getElementById("b1").value;
  const tau = +document.getElementById("cut").value/100;
  const hits= +document.getElementById("hits").value;

  const primes = sievePrimes(b1);
  const steps  = primes.length;
  const cutStep = Math.max(1, Math.floor((1-tau)*steps));
  const y = primes[cutStep-1];

  // rank[p] = pi(p)
  const rank = new Int32Array(b1+1);
  for(let i=0;i<steps;i++) rank[primes[i]] = i+1;

  const lpf = sieveLargestPrimeFactor(b1);
  const BINS = 40;
  const bins = new Float64Array(BINS);
  const cumulative = new Float64Array(steps+1);
  let total = 0, lateCount = 0;
  for(let n=2;n<=b1;n++){
    const r = rank[lpf[n]];
    const idx = r/steps;
    bins[Math.min(BINS-1, Math.floor(idx*BINS))]++;
    cumulative[r]++;
    total++;
    if(r > cutStep) lateCount++;
  }
  for(let i=0;i<BINS;i++) bins[i] /= total;
  let running = 0;
  const cdf = new Float64Array(steps+1);
  for(let r=0;r<=steps;r++){ running += cumulative[r]; cdf[r] = running/total; }

  let median = 1;
  for(let r=0;r<=steps;r++){ if(cdf[r] >= 0.5){ median = r/steps; break; } }

  // model masses
  const integerMass = lateCount/total;
  let recip = 0, factor = 1, nLate = 0;
  for(const p of primes){ if(p>y){ recip += 1/p; factor *= stageExponent(p,b1)+1; nLate++; } }
  const divisorMass = 1 - 1/factor;
  const uniformMass = (steps-cutStep)/steps;

  state.b1=b1; state.tau=tau; state.hits=hits; state.steps=steps; state.y=y;
  state.cutStep=cutStep; state.bins=bins; state.cdf=cdf; state.median=median;
  state.integerMass=integerMass; state.divisorMass=divisorMass;
  state.uniformMass=uniformMass; state.recip=recip; state.factor=factor; state.nLate=nLate;

  document.getElementById("b1v").textContent = b1;
  document.getElementById("stepsv").textContent = steps;
  document.getElementById("cutv").textContent = Math.round(tau*100);
  document.getElementById("yv").textContent = y;
  document.getElementById("hitsv").textContent = hits;
  document.getElementById("latecount").textContent = nLate;
  document.getElementById("latefactor").textContent =
    !isFinite(factor) ? "a number with hundreds of digits"
                      : (factor > 1e15 ? factor.toExponential(2) : factor);

  drawHistogram();
  drawCdf();
  fillTable();
}

function drawHistogram(){
  const c = document.getElementById("hist"), ctx = c.getContext("2d");
  const W=c.width, H=c.height, padL=58, padB=42, padT=16, padR=14;
  ctx.clearRect(0,0,W,H);
  const bins = state.bins, BINS = bins.length;
  const maxV = Math.max(...bins, 1/BINS)*1.08;
  const plotW = W-padL-padR, plotH = H-padT-padB;

  // late window shading
  const x0 = padL + plotW*(1-state.tau);
  ctx.fillStyle="#fed7d7"; ctx.fillRect(x0, padT, padL+plotW-x0, plotH);

  // bars
  for(let i=0;i<BINS;i++){
    const h = bins[i]/maxV*plotH;
    ctx.fillStyle = "#2b6cb0";
    ctx.fillRect(padL + i*plotW/BINS + 1, padT+plotH-h, plotW/BINS - 2, h);
  }
  // uniform reference
  const uh = (1/BINS)/maxV*plotH;
  ctx.strokeStyle="#a0aec0"; ctx.setLineDash([6,4]); ctx.lineWidth=2;
  ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(padL, padT+plotH-uh); ctx.lineTo(padL+plotW, padT+plotH-uh); ctx.stroke();
  ctx.setLineDash([]);

  // axes
  ctx.strokeStyle="#cbd5e0"; ctx.lineWidth=1;
  ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(padL,padT); ctx.lineTo(padL,padT+plotH); ctx.lineTo(padL+plotW,padT+plotH); ctx.stroke();
  ctx.fillStyle="#4a5568"; ctx.font="12px sans-serif"; ctx.textAlign="center";
  for(let t=0;t<=5;t++){
    const frac=t/5;
    ctx.fillText(frac.toFixed(1), padL+plotW*frac, padT+plotH+18);
  }
  ctx.fillText("normalized firing index  \u03C0(P\u207A(n)) / \u03C0(B\u2081)", padL+plotW/2, H-8);
  ctx.textAlign="right";
  ctx.fillText(maxV.toFixed(2), padL-8, padT+10);
  ctx.fillText("0", padL-8, padT+plotH);
  ctx.save(); ctx.translate(14, padT+plotH/2); ctx.rotate(-Math.PI/2);
  ctx.textAlign="center"; ctx.fillText("mass per bin", 0, 0); ctx.restore();
}

function drawCdf(){
  const c = document.getElementById("cdf"), ctx = c.getContext("2d");
  const W=c.width, H=c.height, padL=58, padB=42, padT=16, padR=14;
  ctx.clearRect(0,0,W,H);
  const plotW=W-padL-padR, plotH=H-padT-padB;
  const x0 = padL + plotW*(1-state.tau);
  ctx.fillStyle="#fed7d7"; ctx.fillRect(x0,padT,padL+plotW-x0,plotH);

  ctx.strokeStyle="#a0aec0"; ctx.setLineDash([6,4]); ctx.lineWidth=2;
  ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(padL,padT+plotH); ctx.lineTo(padL+plotW,padT); ctx.stroke();
  ctx.setLineDash([]);

  ctx.strokeStyle="#2f855a"; ctx.lineWidth=2.5; ctx.beginPath();
  for(let r=0;r<=state.steps;r++){
    const x = padL + plotW*(r/state.steps);
    const yy = padT + plotH*(1-state.cdf[r]);
    if(r===0) ctx.moveTo(x,yy); else ctx.lineTo(x,yy);
  }
  ctx.stroke();

  const mx = padL + plotW*state.median;
  ctx.strokeStyle="#dd6b20"; ctx.lineWidth=2; ctx.setLineDash([4,3]);
  ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(mx,padT); ctx.lineTo(mx,padT+plotH); ctx.stroke();
  ctx.setLineDash([]);

  ctx.strokeStyle="#cbd5e0"; ctx.lineWidth=1;
  ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(padL,padT); ctx.lineTo(padL,padT+plotH); ctx.lineTo(padL+plotW,padT+plotH); ctx.stroke();
  ctx.fillStyle="#4a5568"; ctx.font="12px sans-serif"; ctx.textAlign="center";
  for(let t=0;t<=5;t++) ctx.fillText((t/5).toFixed(1), padL+plotW*t/5, padT+plotH+18);
  ctx.fillText("fraction of the schedule consumed", padL+plotW/2, H-8);
  ctx.textAlign="right"; ctx.fillText("1.0", padL-8, padT+10); ctx.fillText("0", padL-8, padT+plotH);

  document.getElementById("summary").innerHTML =
    "At B\u2081 = <b>"+state.b1+"</b> the schedule has <b>"+state.steps+"</b> steps. "+
    "The median order fires after only <b>"+(state.median*100).toFixed(1)+"%</b> of them "+
    "(uniformity would say 50%), and <b>"+((1-state.cdf[Math.floor(0.2*state.steps)])*100).toFixed(1)+
    "%</b> of the mass survives past the first fifth of the schedule.";
}

function fillTable(){
  const rows = [
    ["Divisor model — order uniform among divisors of the multiplier",
     state.divisorMass, "#9b2c2c"],
    ["Uniform law — the pre-registered hypothesis",
     state.uniformMass, "#975a16"],
    ["Integer model — order uniform among the integers (structural law)",
     state.integerMass, "#2f855a"]
  ];
  const body = document.getElementById("models");
  body.innerHTML = "";
  let best = null, bestL = -1;
  for(const [name, mass] of rows.map(r=>[r[0],r[1]])){
    const L = Math.pow(1-mass, state.hits);
    if(L > bestL){ bestL = L; best = name; }
  }
  for(const [name, mass, colour] of rows){
    const L = Math.pow(1-mass, state.hits);
    const tr = document.createElement("tr");
    const verdict = (name === best) ? "selected" : (L < 1e-3 ? "refuted" : "survives");
    tr.innerHTML =
      "<td style='color:"+colour+"'><b>"+name+"</b></td>"+
      "<td>"+(mass*100).toFixed(2)+"%</td>"+
      "<td>"+(L < 1e-4 ? L.toExponential(2) : L.toFixed(5))+"</td>"+
      "<td style='color:"+(verdict==="selected"?"#2f855a":(verdict==="refuted"?"#9b2c2c":"#975a16"))+"'>"+verdict+"</td>";
    body.appendChild(tr);
  }
  const ratio = Math.pow(1-state.integerMass, state.hits) / Math.pow(1-state.uniformMass, state.hits);
  const v = document.getElementById("verdict");
  v.className = "verdict";
  v.innerHTML =
    "Observing <b>0 of "+state.hits+"</b> hits in the last <b>"+Math.round(state.tau*100)+
    "%</b> of the schedule is <b>"+(ratio>1e6?ratio.toExponential(2):Math.round(ratio).toLocaleString())+
    "×</b> more likely under the structural (integer) law than under the pre-registered uniform law "+
    "— and <b>"+(Math.pow(1-state.integerMass,state.hits)/Math.max(Math.pow(1-state.divisorMass,state.hits),1e-300)).toExponential(1)+
    "×</b> more likely than under the divisor model. The reciprocal sum "+
    "\u2211<sub>y<p≤B\u2081</sub> 1/p = <b>"+state.recip.toFixed(4)+
    "</b> is the number doing all the work.";
}

for(const id of ["b1","cut","hits"]){
  document.getElementById(id).addEventListener("input", recompute);
}
recompute();
</script>
</body>
</html>

<body>
<div class="wrap">
  <h1>The Collision-Ceiling Audit</h1>
  <p class="sub">
    Even with no smoothness at all, a run of <em>k</em> guarded modular operations
    has some chance of stumbling onto a multiple of the hidden prime <em>p</em>.
    That <strong>collision baseline</strong> is
    <code>1 − (1 − 1/p)<sup>k</sup></code>, and Bernoulli's inequality
    caps it at <code>k/p</code>. The point of this widget: that cap depends on
    <em>k</em> and <em>p</em> only through their <strong>ratio</strong>. Slide the
    bit length across five orders of magnitude and watch the ceiling refuse to move.
  </p>

  <div class="panel controls">
    <div>
      <label for="bits">Bit length of the hidden prime: <span class="val" id="bitsv">32</span></label>
      <input type="range" id="bits" min="16" max="256" step="1" value="32">
    </div>
    <div>
      <label for="ratio">Stage-one ratio B₁/p = <span class="val" id="ratiov">0.125</span></label>
      <input type="range" id="ratio" min="0.01" max="1.0" step="0.005" value="0.125">
    </div>
    <div>
      <label for="ops">Operations per unit of B₁: <span class="val" id="opsv">2.59</span></label>
      <input type="range" id="ops" min="0.5" max="5" step="0.01" value="2.59">
    </div>
    <div>
      <label for="obs">Observed success rate: <span class="val" id="obsv">62.5</span>%</label>
      <input type="range" id="obs" min="5" max="100" step="0.5" value="62.5">
    </div>
    <div>
      <label for="curves">Curves in the cell: <span class="val" id="curvesv">40</span></label>
      <input type="range" id="curves" min="10" max="200" step="1" value="40">
    </div>
  </div>

  <h2>Scale freedom: the ceiling is a function of k/p alone</h2>
  <div class="panel">
    <canvas id="scale" width="1000" height="280"></canvas>
    <table style="margin-top:14px">
      <thead><tr><th>Quantity</th><th>Value</th><th>Meaning</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody id="rows"></tbody>
    </table>
  </div>

  <h2>Verdict</h2>
  <div class="panel">
    <p id="verdict" class="callout"></p>
    <details>
      <summary>The pigeonhole argument, spelled out</summary>
      <p>
        Let <em>S</em> be the successful curves in a batch and <em>C</em> the
        collision-driven ones. Since <em>S</em> is contained in
        <em>(S \ C) ∪ C</em>, we get
        <code>#(S \ C) ≥ #S − #C</code>. The collision ceiling bounds
        <em>#C</em> from above, so any excess of successes over that bound is a
        guaranteed count of genuine order-hits — successes in which the

### A guided tour of the stage-one firing trace

---

## 0. The question in one sentence

There is a famous algorithm for pulling a medium-sized prime factor out of a
large composite number, and everyone knows *how often* it succeeds. Almost
nobody has asked *when during a run* it succeeds.

This page answers that question. The answer turns out to be a single, sharp
identity — the success moment is the **largest prime factor** of a hidden number
— and everything else on this page is a consequence of it.

You will need no background beyond "primes exist and integers factor uniquely".
Everything harder is tucked behind a fold you can open when you want it.

---

## 1. The setup: a walk through the primes

The [elliptic-curve method of factorization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenstra_elliptic-curve_factorization)
picks a random curve modulo the number $N$ you want to factor, picks a point $P$
on it, and multiplies that point by an enormous integer built out of small
primes. Choose a bound $B_1$ and set

$$K(B_1) \;=\; \prod_{p \le B_1} p^{\lfloor \log_p B_1\rfloor},$$

the product over all primes up to $B_1$ of the largest power of $p$ that still
fits under $B_1$. (This is essentially $\mathrm{lcm}(1,2,\dots,B_1)$.)

Behind the scenes your curve modulo $N$ is secretly a curve modulo each prime
factor $p$ of $N$ at once, and the point $P$ has some order $n$ in the group of
points modulo $p$. If $n$ divides $K(B_1)$, the multiplication kills $P$ modulo
$p$ but not modulo the other factors — the arithmetic breaks in a way that hands
you $p$.

<details>
<summary><b>Why does breaking arithmetic reveal a factor?</b> (click to expand)</summary>

Points on the curve are stored projectively, and adding them requires inverting
a denominator modulo $N$. If the point has become the identity modulo $p$ but
not modulo another prime factor $q$ of $N$, that denominator is divisible by $p$
and not by $N$. The inverse therefore fails to exist — and the greatest common
divisor of the failed denominator with $N$ is a proper factor. The failure
*is* the output.

By [Hasse's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse%27s_theorem_on_elliptic_curves)
the group order lies within $2\sqrt{p}$ of $p+1$, so as you vary the curve, $n$
behaves roughly like a random integer near $p$. Success per curve is then the
probability that such an integer is $B_1$-**smooth** — built only from primes
below $B_1$.
</details>

Crucially, you do not compute $K(B_1)$ and multiply once. You **walk the
schedule**: prime $2$, then $3$, then $5$, then $7$, ..., $\pi(B_1)$ steps in
all. After each step you can ask whether the point has died yet. The fraction of
the schedule consumed when it does is the **firing index**.

---

## 2. Two guesses that both turned out backwards

Before any data were collected, two hypotheses were written down.

> **H1 (shape).** When $B_1$ is small relative to $p$, successes are accidents,
> so the firing index should be *uniform*. When $B_1$ is large, successes are
> genuine "order completion", which should require most of the schedule, so the
> firing index should cluster in the **final 20%**.

> **H2 (rate).** Even with no smoothness, a run of $k$ modular operations has
> some chance of hitting a multiple of $p$ by accident. If the low-$B_1$
> successes were really that accident, the observed success rate should slide
> down toward that baseline as $p$ grows.

Here is what actually happened. At the *generous* setting, where H1's
"grind to the end" story should have been strongest, the median firing index was
**0.09**. Of $55$ recorded successes, the number landing in the final $20\%$ of
the schedule was **zero**. And the success rates at two different scales were
$65.0\%$ and $62.5\%$ — flat, and roughly double the collision baseline.

The clock strikes at the *start*.

---

## 3. The theorem that explains everything

Write $K(B_1, y)$ for the scalar accumulated once the walk has passed $y$:

$$K(B_1, y) \;=\; \prod_{p \le y} p^{\lfloor \log_p B_1\rfloor},$$

and write $P^{+}(n)$ for the largest prime factor of $n$.

> ### The Trace Law
> Let $n$ be an order that stage one can reach at all, i.e. $n \mid K(B_1)$.
> Then for every schedule position $y$,
> $$n \mid K(B_1, y) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad P^{+}(n) \le y .$$

So the firing threshold is *exactly* $P^{+}(n)$, and the normalized firing index
is
$$\mathrm{idx}(n) \;=\; \frac{\pi\big(P^{+}(n)\big)}{\pi(B_1)} .$$

Everything else about $n$ — its size, how many prime factors it has, their
multiplicities — is invisible in the trace.

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal the proof.</b> It is four lines, and it is the whole story.</summary>

**($\Rightarrow$)** If $n$ divides the partial product, so does its largest
prime factor. But every prime dividing $K(B_1,y)$ is one of the schedule primes
$\le y$ — because a prime dividing a product of prime powers must equal one of
those primes. Hence $P^{+}(n) \le y$.

**($\Leftarrow$)** Suppose $P^{+}(n) \le y$. Split the full multiplier at the
cut, $K(B_1) = A \cdot B$, where $A$ collects the primes $\le y$ and $B$ the
primes $> y$. Every prime in $B$ exceeds $y \ge P^{+}(n)$, so it does not divide
$n$; hence $\gcd(n, B) = 1$. Since $n \mid AB$ and $n$ is coprime to $B$, we get
$n \mid A$ — and $A$ divides $K(B_1, y)$. $\blacksquare$

The subtle point is the *maximality of the exponents*: by the time the walk has
passed $p$, the scalar already contains $p$ to the highest power stage one will
ever supply. There is no gradual accretion to wait for. That is why the firing
moment collapses to a single prime.
</details>

Now recall a classical fact: **the largest prime factor of a random integer is
usually small.** Half of all integers are even; only one in $97$ is divisible by
$97$. An order whose largest prime factor sits among the last few schedule
primes is rare by construction. This is
[Dickman–Golomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dickman_function) territory, and
it is exactly what the trace measures.

## 5. Why the late tail is thin: a sieve in one line

If a curve fires *late* — after position $y$ — the trace law says its order must
be divisible by some prime in the window $(y, B_1]$. Count the multiples of each
such prime below $M$ and add:

$$\#\{\text{late firers} \le M\} \;\le\; \sum_{y < p \le B_1} \Big\lfloor \frac{M}{p} \Big\rfloor \;\le\; M \sum_{y<p\le B_1} \frac{1}{p}.$$

That is it. The late tail is a **reciprocal sum of large primes**, and those are
tiny.

<details>
<summary><b>The concrete case $B_1 = 100$ — and why the bound is nearly exact</b></summary>

At $B_1 = 100$ the schedule has $\pi(100) = 25$ steps. Cut at $y = 67$: the
primes beyond the cut are $71, 73, 79, 83, 89, 97$ — the final **six** steps,
$24\%$ of the schedule. Their reciprocal sum is

$$\tfrac1{71}+\tfrac1{73}+\tfrac1{79}+\tfrac1{83}+\tfrac1{89}+\tfrac1{97} = 0.0740 < \tfrac{2}{25} = 0.08 .$$

Eight percent, where uniformity demands twenty-four.

And the bound is *exact* in the short range. If $M \le y^2$, no integer below
$M$ can be divisible by two distinct primes above $y$ — their product would
already exceed $y^2 \ge M$. So the union is disjoint and the inequality is an
equality. Concretely, among the $4489 = 67^2$ integers in $(0, 67^2]$, exactly
$330$ fire late: a density of $7.35\%$.

The pre-registered $20\%$ was never on the table.
</details>

## 6. The rival theory, and how it lost

Here is the genuinely interesting twist. There was a competing account, and it
was not stupid.

When people worry about "collision-contaminated accounting", they implicitly
model the order not as a random *integer* but as a random *divisor of the
multiplier* $K(B_1)$. That is a completely different distribution — and by the
trace law we can compute exactly what it predicts:

$$\tau\big(K(B_1)\big) \;=\; \tau\big(K(B_1,y)\big)\cdot \prod_{y<p\le B_1}\big(\lfloor\log_p B_1\rfloor+1\big).$$

At $B_1 = 100$, $y = 67$ each of the six late primes contributes a factor of
$2$, so the local factor is $2^6 = 64$: the divisor model says **$63/64 \approx 98\%$**
of the mass lands in the final six steps.

So the two models make *opposite* predictions about the same measurement:
$8\%$ versus $98\%$. The empty tail annihilates one of them.

{{algorithm:2}}

<details>
<summary><b>The likelihood arithmetic</b></summary>

With $55$ recorded hits and none in the late window:

| account | late mass | likelihood of an empty tail |
|---|---|---|
| divisor model | $63/64$ | $(1/64)^{55} \approx 4.6\times10^{-100}$ |
| uniform law | $0.20$ | $(4/5)^{55} \approx 4.7\times10^{-6}$ |
| structural (integer) law | $\le 2/25$ | $\ge (23/25)^{55} \approx 1.0\times10^{-2}$ |

The structural law is more than $2000\times$ likelier than uniformity and
astronomically likelier than the divisor model. The measurement does not merely
reject a hypothesis — it *selects a model*: for the purposes of the firing
trace, the order behaves like a random **integer**, not like a random divisor.
</details>

---

## 7. And it only gets worse for uniformity

The $B_1 = 100$ computation is one data point. The general theorem removes the
numbers entirely, and it leans on a lovely old estimate of Erdős: the product of
all primes up to $y$ never exceeds $4^{y}$.

<details>
<summary><b>From the primorial bound to a vanishing tail</b></summary>

Let $k$ be the number of primes in $(y, B_1]$. Each exceeds $y$, so their
product is at least $y^{k}$; and their product divides the primorial of $B_1$,
so it is at most $4^{B_1}$. Since $2^{\lfloor\log_2 y\rfloor} \le y$,

$$2^{\,k\lfloor \log_2 y\rfloor} \le y^{k} \le 4^{B_1} = 2^{2B_1},$$

so $k \cdot \lfloor\log_2 y\rfloor \le 2B_1$. Combine with the sieve bound:

$$\text{late density} \;\le\; \frac{2B_1}{y\,\lfloor \log_2 y\rfloor}.$$

Put the cut at half the stage-one bound and this is $4/\lfloor\log_2 y\rfloor$,
which **tends to zero**. A constant-fraction late tail is not merely
unobserved — it is impossible for all large $B_1$.
</details>

## 8. The other hypothesis: collisions

Now the rate side. Even with no smoothness, a run of $k$ guarded operations
modulo $p$ hits a multiple of $p$ with probability $1 - (1-1/p)^{k}$. Bernoulli's
inequality caps that:

$$1 - \left(1-\frac1p\right)^{k} \;\le\; \frac{k}{p}.$$

Stare at the right-hand side. It depends on $k$ and $p$ **only through their
ratio** — the baseline is *scale free*. Since the experiment fixes $B_1/p$ and
sets $k = c\,B_1$, the ratio $k/p = c\,(B_1/p)$ is invariant by construction.
A collision-dominated account therefore predicts **exactly the same** ceiling at
every bit length, so it cannot possibly predict the collapse H2 asserted.

Drag the bit-length slider below across four octaves and watch the baseline
curve refuse to move.

What *does* discriminate is the level. Honest accounting puts the operation

thirty-point gap cannot be collisions at any scale, and pigeonhole turns it into
a count: in a cell of $40$ curves with $25$ successes, at most $12$ can be

## 10. What is left open

The trace law converts a *positional* question about an algorithm's ladder into
a *reciprocal sum over primes*. Reciprocal sums over primes are the domain of
[Mertens' theorems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mertens%27_theorems), which
suggests a sharp asymptotic:

> ### Conjecture (Mertens Firing-Tail Law)
> For a cut at the $(1-\tau)$-quantile of the schedule,
> $$\mathrm{tail}(\tau, B_1) \;=\; \frac{\log\big(1/(1-\tau)\big)}{\log B_1}\big(1+o(1)\big).$$

At $\tau = 0.2$ and $B_1 = 10^6$ this predicts $0.0162$. Direct computation
gives $0.016$.

Other threads worth pulling: extending exactness of the sieve beyond the range
$M \le y^2$ with a second-order inclusion–exclusion term; replacing Erdős'
$4^{B_1}$ with an effective Chebyshev bound to sharpen the constant; extending
the law to the continuation phase, where a single extra large prime is allowed;
quantifying how elliptic-curve group orders, biased by torsion, deviate from
uniform integers; and the practical payoff — if nine-tenths of the firing mass
lies in the first fifth of the schedule, a *fractional* run captures nearly all
the hits of a full one, which turns budget allocation into a tractable
optimization.

---

## 11. The one-line summary

**A factoring run's moment of luck is the largest prime factor of a number it
never sees.** Largest prime factors of random integers are almost always small.
That is why this clock always strikes early — and why two perfectly reasonable
hypotheses about its timing were both exactly backwards.

import Novelty.SmoothNumberLowerBound

namespace Catalog.Novelty.EcmStageOneTraceLaw

open Finset Catalog.Novelty.SmoothNumberLowerBound

/-! ### The stage-1 schedule -/

/-- The primes at most `y`, i.e. the prefix of the ECM stage-1 schedule that has
been consumed once the schedule reaches `y`. -/
def primesUpTo (y : ℕ) : Finset ℕ := (range (y + 1)).filter Nat.Prime

/-- The accumulated stage-1 scalar after the schedule has consumed all primes
`p ≤ y`: `∏_{p ≤ y} p ^ ⌊log_p B1⌋`.  For `y ≥ B1` this is the full stage-1
multiplier `K(B1) = lcm(1, …, B1)`. -/
def stageProd (B1 y : ℕ) : ℕ := ∏ p ∈ primesUpTo y, p ^ Nat.log p B1

/-- The largest prime factor of `n` (`0` for `n = 0, 1`). -/
def maxPF (n : ℕ) : ℕ := n.primeFactors.sup id

/-- The number of schedule steps consumed before an order `n` fires. -/
def stepIndex (n : ℕ) : ℕ := #(primesUpTo (maxPF n))

/-- The total number of schedule steps, `π(B1)`. -/
def totalSteps (B1 : ℕ) : ℕ := #(primesUpTo B1)

lemma mem_primesUpTo {y p : ℕ} : p ∈ primesUpTo y ↔ p ≤ y ∧ p.Prime := by
  simp [primesUpTo]

lemma stageProd_pos (B1 y : ℕ) : 0 < stageProd B1 y := by
  refine Finset.prod_pos fun p hp => ?_
  exact pow_pos (mem_primesUpTo.mp hp).2.pos _

lemma primesUpTo_mono {y z : ℕ} (h : y ≤ z) : primesUpTo y ⊆ primesUpTo z := by
  intro p hp
  exact mem_primesUpTo.mpr ⟨le_trans (mem_primesUpTo.mp hp).1 h, (mem_primesUpTo.mp hp).2⟩

lemma stageProd_dvd_mono {B1 y z : ℕ} (h : y ≤ z) : stageProd B1 y ∣ stageProd B1 z :=
  Finset.prod_dvd_prod_of_subset _ _ _ (primesUpTo_mono h)

/-! ### Basic facts about the largest prime factor -/

lemma maxPF_prime {n : ℕ} (hn : n.primeFactors.Nonempty) : (maxPF n).Prime := by
  obtain ⟨p, hp, hmax⟩ := Finset.exists_mem_eq_sup n.primeFactors hn id
  rw [maxPF, hmax]
  exact Nat.prime_of_mem_primeFactors hp

lemma maxPF_dvd {n : ℕ} (hn : n.primeFactors.Nonempty) : maxPF n ∣ n := by
  obtain ⟨p, hp, hmax⟩ := Finset.exists_mem_eq_sup n.primeFactors hn id
  rw [maxPF, hmax]
  exact Nat.dvd_of_mem_primeFactors hp

lemma le_maxPF {n p : ℕ} (hp : p ∈ n.primeFactors) : p ≤ maxPF n :=
  Finset.le_sup (f := id) hp

lemma primeFactors_nonempty_of_maxPF {n : ℕ} (h : 0 < maxPF n) : n.primeFactors.Nonempty := by
  by_contra hne
  rw [Finset.not_nonempty_iff_eq_empty] at hne
  simp [maxPF, hne] at h

/-! ### The trace law -/

/-- Every prime factor of a stage-1 partial product is a schedule prime `≤ y`. -/
lemma prime_dvd_stageProd_le {B1 y p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (h : p ∣ stageProd B1 y) : p ≤ y := by
  rw [stageProd] at h
  obtain ⟨q, hq, hpq⟩ := (Nat.Prime.prime hp).exists_mem_finset_dvd h
  have := hp.dvd_of_dvd_pow hpq
  have hqp : q.Prime := (mem_primesUpTo.mp hq).2
  rw [(Nat.prime_dvd_prime_iff_eq hp hqp).mp this]
  exact (mem_primesUpTo.mp hq).1

/-- **The trace law.**  A stage-1 reachable order `n` divides the partial
product at `y` exactly when its largest prime factor is at most `y`.  The firing
moment carries no information beyond `maxPF n`. -/
theorem dvd_stageProd_iff_maxPF_le {B1 y n : ℕ} (hn : n ≠ 0) (hreach : n ∣ stageProd B1 B1) :
    n ∣ stageProd B1 y ↔ maxPF n ≤ y := by
  constructor
  · intro h
    by_cases h1 : n = 1
    · simp [maxPF, h1]
    · have hne : n.primeFactors.Nonempty := by
        rw [Finset.nonempty_iff_ne_empty]
        intro hcon
        exact h1 (by simpa [Nat.primeFactors_eq_empty, hn] using hcon)
      exact prime_dvd_stageProd_le (maxPF_prime hne) ((maxPF_dvd hne).trans h)
  · intro hle
    -- split the full product at `y`; `n` is coprime to the tail
    have hsplit :
        (∏ p ∈ primesUpTo B1 with p ≤ y, p ^ Nat.log p B1) *
          (∏ p ∈ primesUpTo B1 with ¬ p ≤ y, p ^ Nat.log p B1) = stageProd B1 B1 :=
      Finset.prod_filter_mul_prod_filter_not _ _ _
    have hcop : Nat.Coprime n (∏ p ∈ primesUpTo B1 with ¬ p ≤ y, p ^ Nat.log p B1) := by
      refine Nat.Coprime.prod_right fun p hp => ?_
      rw [Finset.mem_filter] at hp
      have hpp : p.Prime := (mem_primesUpTo.mp hp.1).2
      refine Nat.Coprime.pow_right _ ?_
      rw [Nat.coprime_comm]
      refine (Nat.Prime.coprime_iff_not_dvd hpp).mpr fun hdvd => ?_
      have : p ∈ n.primeFactors := Nat.mem_primeFactors.mpr ⟨hpp, hdvd, hn⟩
      exact hp.2 (le_trans (le_maxPF this) hle)
    have hdvd1 : n ∣ ∏ p ∈ primesUpTo B1 with p ≤ y, p ^ Nat.log p B1 := by
      refine hcop.dvd_of_dvd_mul_right ?_
      rw [hsplit]; exact hreach
    refine hdvd1.trans (Finset.prod_dvd_prod_of_subset _ _ _ ?_)
    intro p hp
    rw [Finset.mem_filter] at hp
    exact mem_primesUpTo.mpr ⟨hp.2, (mem_primesUpTo.mp hp.1).2⟩

/-- The firing threshold of a stage-1 reachable order is *exactly* its largest
prime factor: it is the least `y` at which the accumulated scalar annihilates
the point. -/
theorem isLeast_fireY {B1 n : ℕ} (hn : n ≠ 0) (hreach : n ∣ stageProd B1 B1) :
    IsLeast {y | n ∣ stageProd B1 y} (maxPF n) := by
  refine ⟨(dvd_stageProd_iff_maxPF_le hn hreach).mpr le_rfl, fun y hy => ?_⟩
  exact (dvd_stageProd_iff_maxPF_le hn hreach).mp hy

/-- The normalized firing index is `π(maxPF n) / π(B1)`: a function of the
largest prime factor alone. -/
theorem stepIndex_eq {B1 n : ℕ} (hn : n ≠ 0) (hreach : n ∣ stageProd B1 B1) :
    stepIndex n = #(primesUpTo (sInf {y | n ∣ stageProd B1 y})) := by
  have h := isLeast_fireY hn hreach
  rw [stepIndex, ← h.csInf_eq]

/-- Firing is monotone in the largest prime factor: a smaller largest prime
factor fires no later. -/
theorem stepIndex_mono {m n : ℕ} (h : maxPF m ≤ maxPF n) : stepIndex m ≤ stepIndex n :=
  Finset.card_mono (primesUpTo_mono h)

/-! ### The late tail is structurally thin (refutation of H1) -/

/-- **Late firing forces a large prime.**  If a stage-1 reachable order has not
fired by the time the schedule has passed `y`, then it is divisible by a prime in
`(y, B1]` — one of the catalog's `largePrimes B1 y`. -/
theorem late_fire_large_prime_dvd {B1 y n : ℕ} (hn : n ≠ 0) (hreach : n ∣ stageProd B1 B1)
    (hlate : ¬ n ∣ stageProd B1 y) : ∃ p ∈ largePrimes B1 y, p ∣ n := by
  have hgt : y < maxPF n := by
    by_contra hcon
    exact hlate ((dvd_stageProd_iff_maxPF_le hn hreach).mpr (not_lt.mp hcon))
  have hne : n.primeFactors.Nonempty := primeFactors_nonempty_of_maxPF (by omega)
  have hple : maxPF n ≤ B1 :=
    prime_dvd_stageProd_le (maxPF_prime hne) ((maxPF_dvd hne).trans hreach)
  exact ⟨maxPF n, by
      simp only [largePrimes, Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_Ioc]
      exact ⟨⟨hgt, hple⟩, maxPF_prime hne⟩, maxPF_dvd hne⟩

/-- The set of orders in `(0, M]` that fire in the part of the schedule beyond
`y`, i.e. that are divisible by some prime of `largePrimes B1 y`. -/
def lateOrders (M B1 y : ℕ) : Finset ℕ :=
  {n ∈ Ioc 0 M | ∃ p ∈ largePrimes B1 y, p ∣ n}

/-- **Sieve bound on the late tail.**  At most `∑_{y < p ≤ B1} ⌊M/p⌋` of the
orders in `(0, M]` can fire beyond schedule position `y`.  (Same union bound the
catalog's `L_lower_sieve` uses, transported to the trace side.) -/
theorem lateCount_le_primeContribution (M B1 y : ℕ) :
    #(lateOrders M B1 y) ≤ ∑ p ∈ largePrimes B1 y, M / p := by
  have hsub : lateOrders M B1 y ⊆
      (largePrimes B1 y).biUnion (fun p => {n ∈ Ioc 0 M | p ∣ n}) := by
    intro n hn
    simp only [lateOrders, Finset.mem_filter] at hn
    obtain ⟨hmem, p, hp, hpn⟩ := hn
    exact Finset.mem_biUnion.mpr ⟨p, hp, Finset.mem_filter.mpr ⟨hmem, hpn⟩⟩
  refine le_trans (Finset.card_mono hsub) (le_trans (Finset.card_biUnion_le) ?_)
  exact le_of_eq (Finset.sum_congr rfl fun p _ => Nat.Ioc_filter_dvd_card_eq_div M p)

/-- All orders that fire strictly after schedule position `y` lie in
`lateOrders`. -/
theorem lateOrders_of_late {M B1 y n : ℕ} (hn : n ≠ 0) (hnM : n ≤ M)
    (hreach : n ∣ stageProd B1 B1) (hlate : ¬ n ∣ stageProd B1 y) :
    n ∈ lateOrders M B1 y := by
  simp only [lateOrders, Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_Ioc]
  exact ⟨⟨Nat.pos_of_ne_zero hn, hnM⟩, late_fire_large_prime_dvd hn hreach hlate⟩

/-! #### The concrete instance `B1 = 100` -/

lemma totalSteps_hundred : totalSteps 100 = 25 := by decide

lemma steps_sixtySeven : #(primesUpTo 67) = 19 := by decide

/-- At `B1 = 100` the primes past position `67` are exactly the last six schedule
steps, i.e. the final `6/25 = 24%` of the schedule. -/
lemma largePrimes_hundred : largePrimes 100 67 = {71, 73, 79, 83, 89, 97} := by decide

/-- The reciprocal sum of the late primes is below `2/25`: the *structural*
probability that a random order fires in the final quarter of the `B1 = 100`
schedule. -/
lemma late_reciprocal_sum_lt : ∑ p ∈ largePrimes 100 67, (1 : ℝ) / p < 2 / 25 := by
  rw [largePrimes_hundred]
  norm_num

/-- **Refutation of H1 at `B1 = 100`.**  The number of orders in `(0, M]` that
can fire in the final `24%` of the stage-1 schedule is less than `2M/25 = 0.08 M`
— far below the `0.2 M` that a *uniform* firing index would predict, and
consistent with the measured empty tail (`0/55`).  Uniformity of the firing-step
index is not merely unobserved: it is structurally impossible. -/

  have h2 : ∑ p ∈ largePrimes 100 67, ((M / p : ℕ) : ℝ)

    refine Finset.sum_le_sum fun p hp => ?_
    have hp0 : 0 < p := by
      have := (Finset.mem_filter.mp hp).2
      exact this.pos
    have := Nat.cast_div_le (α := ℝ) (m := M) (n := p)
    calc ((M / p : ℕ) : ℝ) ≤ (M : ℝ) / (p : ℝ) := this
      _ = (M : ℝ) * (1 / p) := by ring

      = (M : ℝ) * ∑ p ∈ largePrimes 100 67, (1 : ℝ) / p := by

    _ = 2 / 25 * M := by ring

/-! ### Work-weighted version of the trace law -/

/-- Each schedule prime contributes a factor at most `B1`, so the accumulated
scalar at position `y` is at most `B1 ^ π(y)`: in *work* units too, an order with
a small largest prime factor fires early. -/
theorem stageProd_le_pow (B1 y : ℕ) (hB1 : B1 ≠ 0) :
    stageProd B1 y ≤ B1 ^ #(primesUpTo y) := by
  rw [stageProd, ← Finset.prod_const]
  exact Finset.prod_le_prod' fun p _ => Nat.pow_log_le_self p hB1

/-- The full stage-1 multiplier dominates the primorial: every prime `≤ B1`
occurs at least once. -/
theorem primorial_dvd_stageProd (B1 : ℕ) :
    (∏ p ∈ primesUpTo B1, p) ∣ stageProd B1 B1 := by
  refine Finset.prod_dvd_prod_of_dvd _ _ fun p hp => ?_
  have hpp : p.Prime := (mem_primesUpTo.mp hp).2
  have hle : p ≤ B1 := (mem_primesUpTo.mp hp).1
  have : 1 ≤ Nat.log p B1 := Nat.log_pos hpp.one_lt hle
  exact dvd_pow_self p (by omega)

/-! ### The collision baseline (refutation of H2) -/

/-- The random-collision success probability of a stage-1 run of `k` guarded
group operations modulo `p`: `1 - (1 - 1/p)^k`. -/
noncomputable def collisionProb (p k : ℕ) : ℝ := 1 - (1 - 1 / (p : ℝ)) ^ k

/-- **Bernoulli ceiling.**  The collision baseline never exceeds `k/p`. -/
theorem collisionProb_le_ratio {p k : ℕ} (hp : 0 < p) : collisionProb p k ≤ k / p := by
  have hp0 : (0 : ℝ) < p := by exact_mod_cast hp
  have hge : (-2 : ℝ) ≤ -(1 / p) := by
    have : (1 : ℝ) / p ≤ 1 := by
      rw [div_le_one hp0]
      exact_mod_cast hp
    linarith
  have := one_add_mul_le_pow hge k
  have hrw : (1 : ℝ) + (-(1 / p)) = 1 - 1 / p := by ring
  rw [hrw] at this
  rw [collisionProb]
  have : 1 - (1 - 1 / (p : ℝ)) ^ k ≤ 1 - (1 + (k : ℝ) * (-(1 / p))) := by linarith
  calc 1 - (1 - 1 / (p : ℝ)) ^ k ≤ 1 - (1 + (k : ℝ) * (-(1 / p))) := this
    _ = (k : ℝ) / p := by field_simp; ring

/-- **Scale freedom of the collision baseline (H2 is untestable by bit length).**
The ceiling depends only on the *ratio* `k/p`.  Two runs at different bit
lengths but the same ratio share the same ceiling, so the collision hypothesis
predicts *no* cross-bit-length collapse — exactly what was measured
(`z`-test `p = 0.8161`). -/
theorem collision_ceiling_scale_free {p q k l : ℕ} (hp : 0 < p) (hq : 0 < q)
    (h : (k : ℝ) / p = (l : ℝ) / q) :
    collisionProb p k ≤ (l : ℝ) / q ∧ collisionProb q l ≤ (k : ℝ) / p := by
  refine ⟨?_, ?_⟩
  · rw [← h]; exact collisionProb_le_ratio hp
  · rw [h]; exact collisionProb_le_ratio hq

/-- **The measured operating point.**  With `B1/p = 0.125` and the honest op
count `ops = 2.59 · B1` (rather than the `1.44` constant used in the original
pre-registration), the collision ceiling is at most `0.324` for *every* prime
`p`, while the measured success rate is `0.625`: the excess `0.3` is not
explicable by collisions at any scale. -/
theorem collision_subdominant {p k : ℕ} (hp : 0 < p) (hk : (k : ℝ) ≤ 0.324 * p)
    {obs : ℝ} (hobs : 0.625 ≤ obs) : collisionProb p k + 0.3 ≤ obs := by
  have hp0 : (0 : ℝ) < p := by exact_mod_cast hp
  have h1 : collisionProb p k ≤ (k : ℝ) / p := collisionProb_le_ratio hp
  have h2 : (k : ℝ) / p ≤ 0.324 := by
    rw [div_le_iff₀ hp0]; linarith
  linarith

/-- **Pigeonhole: genuine order-hits must exist.**  In a batch `T` of curves with
success set `S` and collision set `C`, at least `#S - #C` of the successes are

theorem order_hits_card_lower_bound {α : Type*} [DecidableEq α] (S C : Finset α) :
    #S - #C ≤ #(S \ C) := by
  have : #S ≤ #(S \ C) + #C := by
    calc #S ≤ #((S \ C) ∪ C) := Finset.card_mono (by
          intro x hx
          by_cases hxc : x ∈ C
          · exact Finset.mem_union_right _ hxc
          · exact Finset.mem_union_left _ (Finset.mem_sdiff.mpr ⟨hx, hxc⟩))
      _ ≤ #(S \ C) + #C := Finset.card_union_le _ _
  omega

/-- The concrete cell of exp 570: `#S = 25` successes out of 40 curves, at most

real but subdominant. -/

    (hS : #S = 25) (hC : #C ≤ 12) : 13 ≤ #(S \ C) := by
  have := order_hits_card_lower_bound S C
  omega

  "future_directions": "# FUTURE DIRECTIONS — the stage-one firing trace

## What this cycle established

Three strands of theory now stand behind the measured trace, all fully proved.

**1. The trace law.** For a stage-one reachable order $n$ (one dividing the full
multiplier $K(B_1)$) and any schedule cut $y$,
$$n \mid K(B_1, y) \iff P^{+}(n) \le y,$$
so the firing threshold is *exactly* the largest prime factor and the normalized
firing index is $\pi(P^{+}(n))/\pi(B_1)$. Consequences: late firing forces a
large prime divisor in $(y, B_1]$; a sieve/union bound caps the late-firing count
in $(0,M]$ by $\sum_{y<p\le B_1}\lfloor M/p\rfloor$; and at $B_1 = 100$ the final
six of the twenty-five schedule steps are reachable by density below $0.08$, not
the $0.2$ of the pre-registered uniformity hypothesis. On the rate side, the
Bernoulli ceiling $1-(1-1/p)^k \le k/p$ is *scale free*, so the collision
hypothesis cannot predict a cross-bit-length collapse; at the measured operating
point it leaves a $0.3$ gap to the observed rate, which pigeonholes into at least
thirteen genuine order-hits per forty-curve cell.

**2. The exact firing law of the competing null model.** Divisors of $K(B_1)$
firing by $y$ are exactly divisors of the partial multiplier $K(B_1,y)$, giving
$$\tau(K(B_1)) = \tau(K(B_1,y)) \cdot \prod_{y<p\le B_1}\big(\lfloor \log_p B_1\rfloor + 1\big).$$
At $B_1 = 100$ that factor is $64$, so the divisor model puts $63/64 \approx 98\%$
of the mass in the last six steps — the opposite prediction to the integer model,
which caps the same window at $8\%$. The measured $0/55$ empty tail is more than
$1000\times$ more likely under the structural law than under uniformity.

**3. The asymptotic form.** From Erdős' bound $B_1\# \le 4^{B_1}$ one gets the
Chebyshev-type count $\#\{p : y < p \le B_1\}\cdot\lfloor\log_2 y\rfloor \le 2B_1$,
hence the unconditional density bound $\#\text{lateOrders} \le M\cdot 2B_1/(y\lfloor\log_2 y\rfloor)$
and the decay $\le 4M/\lfloor\log_2 y\rfloor$ for a cut at half the bound. A
constant-fraction late tail is impossible for large $B_1$.

Measured trace statistics match: medians $0.083 \to 0.006$ for $N = 10^3 \to 10^6$,
final-$20\%$ mass $3.4\% \to 1.6\%$.

## Conjectures for the next cycle

### 1. Mertens Firing-Tail Law

For a cut at the $(1-\tau)$-quantile of the schedule, the late-firing density
should satisfy
$$\mathrm{tail}(\tau, B_1) = \frac{\log\big(1/(1-\tau)\big)}{\log B_1}\,\big(1 + o(1)\big).$$
The key insight is that the trace law converts a *positional* question about the
stage-one ladder into the Mertens sum $\sum_{y<p\le B_1} 1/p$, whose value across
a $(1-\tau)B_1$-to-$B_1$ window is $\log\big(\log B_1/\log((1-\tau)B_1)\big)
\approx \log(1/(1-\tau))/\log B_1$. Proving it requires an effective Mertens
estimate over the truncated range, control of the quantile-to-value conversion,
and an inclusion–exclusion correction beyond the short range $M \le y^2$ where
multiple large prime divisors become possible.

### 2. Beyond the short range

Exactness of the union bound currently holds only for $M \le y^2$. A second-order
term $-\sum_{y<p<q\le B_1}\lfloor M/pq\rfloor$ should extend exactness to
$M \le y^3$, and a full Legendre-type expansion should give the tail to all
orders.

### 3. Sharpening the Chebyshev input

Replacing Erdős' $4^{B_1}$ by an effective Chebyshev bound $\theta(x) < 1.001102\,x$
would improve the constant in the late-density bound from $2$ to roughly
$1.45/\log 2$, tightening the decay statement correspondingly.

### 4. Stage two

The continuation phase admits a single extra large prime beyond $B_1$. The trace
law should extend to a two-parameter statement in which the firing threshold is
governed jointly by the largest and second-largest prime factors, with the late
tail controlled by a two-dimensional Dickman-type region.

### 5. Order-population bias

Elliptic-curve group orders are not uniform integers: they are biased by torsion
structure and by curve construction. Quantifying the deviation of largest-prime-factor
statistics on that population from the uniform-integer baseline would sharpen
every density estimate in this cycle.

### 6. Early-abort scheduling

If nine-tenths of the firing mass lies in the first fifth of the schedule, a
*fractional* stage-one run captures most of the hits of a full run. Allocating a
fixed operation budget across curves and schedule fractions becomes a concrete
optimization problem that the trace law makes tractable.

### 7. Trace as a runtime diagnostic

Because the firing index reads off $\pi(P^{+}(n))/\pi(B_1)$, an observed trace is
a direct measurement of the largest prime factor of the hidden group order —
usable to re-tune the stage-one bound adaptively mid-computation.

    "demo": """"
demo.py — Numerical demonstration of the stage-one firing trace law.

This script is a fully self-contained numerical companion to the theory of the
*firing trace* of the first stage of the elliptic-curve factorization method.

Background in one paragraph
---------------------------
Stage one of the elliptic-curve method walks through the primes
p_1 < p_2 < ... < p_{pi(B1)} up to a bound B1, and after each prime multiplies
an accumulating scalar by p^{floor(log_p B1)}.  Writing

    K(B1, y) = prod_{p <= y} p^{floor(log_p B1)},

the run "fires" for a point of order n at the first schedule position y where
n divides K(B1, y).  The *trace law* says that for any order n dividing the full
multiplier K(B1, B1),

    n | K(B1, y)   <==>   P+(n) <= y,

where P+(n) is the largest prime factor of n.  So the firing threshold equals
P+(n) exactly, and the *normalized firing index* is pi(P+(n)) / pi(B1).

Because a typical integer has a small largest prime factor relative to its own
size (Dickman/Golomb statistics), the firing index piles up near 0 and the late
tail of the schedule is almost empty.  This is the structural reason a
pre-registered hypothesis predicting a *uniform* firing index, or a firing index
concentrated in the final 20% of the schedule, is refuted by data.

What this script demonstrates
-----------------------------
 1. Direct verification of the trace law on all divisors of K(B1, B1).
 2. The empirical firing-index distribution for uniform orders in (0, N],
    for N = 10^3 ... 10^6, reproducing medians 0.083 -> 0.005 and a final-20%
    tail decaying 3.4% -> 1.5%.
 3. The exact late-tail count at B1 = 100 with the schedule cut at y = 67:
    exactly 330 of the 4489 integers in (0, 67^2] fire in the last six of the
    25 schedule steps (7.35%), versus the 20% a uniform law demands.
 4. The competing *divisor* null model: the number of divisors of K(B1) splits
    as tau(K_y) times prod_{y < p <= B1} (floor(log_p B1) + 1); at B1 = 100,
    y = 67 that factor is 64, so the divisor model puts 63/64 ~ 98% of its mass
    in exactly the window the integer model caps at 8%.
 5. The likelihood of the observed empty tail (0 hits out of 55) under the two
    laws, and the resulting likelihood ratio (> 1000 in favour of the
    structural law).
 6. The collision-baseline side: the Bernoulli ceiling 1 - (1 - 1/p)^k <= k/p,
    its scale freedom in the ratio k/p, and the pigeonhole lower bound on the
    number of genuine order-hits in a batch of curves.
 7. The unconditional asymptotic bound: the late-firing density is at most
    2*B1 / (y * floor(log2 y)), hence O(1 / log B1) for a cut proportional
    to B1 -- no constant-fraction late tail can survive.

Run with:  python3 demo.py
No third-party dependencies.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Dict, Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Elementary sieves
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def primes_up_to(n: int) -> List[int]:
    """All primes p <= n, by a simple sieve of Eratosthenes.  O(n log log n)."""
    if n < 2:
        return []
    sieve = bytearray([1]) * (n + 1)
    sieve[0] = sieve[1] = 0
    for p in range(2, int(n**0.5) + 1):
        if sieve[p]:
            sieve[p * p :: p] = bytearray(len(sieve[p * p :: p]))
    return [i for i in range(n + 1) if sieve[i]]


def largest_prime_factor_table(n: int) -> List[int]:
    """largest_prime_factor_table(n)[m] = P+(m), the largest prime factor of m.

    Entries for m = 0 and m = 1 are 0 by convention.  Computed by sweeping each
    prime p over its multiples, so the last prime written for m is the largest.
    Cost O(n log log n) time, O(n) memory.
    """
    lpf = [0] * (n + 1)
    for p in range(2, n + 1):
        if lpf[p] == 0:  # p is prime
            for multiple in range(p, n + 1, p):
                lpf[multiple] = p
    return lpf


def prime_counting(n: int, primes: Sequence[int]) -> int:
    """pi(n), given a sorted list of primes covering [0, n]."""
    lo, hi = 0, len(primes)
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if primes[mid] <= n:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid
    return lo


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. The stage-one schedule
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def stage_product(b1: int, y: int) -> int:
    """K(B1, y) = prod_{p <= y} p^{floor(log_p B1)}: the accumulated scalar
    after the stage-one schedule has consumed every prime up to y."""
    result = 1
    for p in primes_up_to(min(y, b1)):
        exponent = int(math.log(b1) / math.log(p) + 1e-12)
        result *= p**exponent
    return result


def max_prime_factor(n: int) -> int:
    """P+(n) by trial division; 0 for n in {0, 1}."""
    if n <= 1:
        return 0
    best, m, d = 1, n, 2
    while d * d <= m:
        while m % d == 0:
            best, m = d, m // d
        d += 1
    return max(best, m)


def stage_exponents(b1: int, y: int) -> Dict[int, int]:
    """The exponent vector of K(B1, y): p -> floor(log_p B1) for each p <= y."""
    return {p: int(math.log(b1) / math.log(p) + 1e-12)
            for p in primes_up_to(min(y, b1))}


def divisor_count(exponents: Dict[int, int]) -> int:
    """tau of a number given as a prime-exponent vector: prod (e_p + 1)."""
    total = 1
    for exponent in exponents.values():
        total *= exponent + 1
    return total


def divisors_with_max_prime(exponents: Dict[int, int]) -> Iterable[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """Enumerate every divisor of the number with the given prime-exponent
    vector, together with its largest prime factor (0 for the divisor 1).
    Enumerating from the exponent vector avoids any factorization work."""
    items: List[Tuple[int, int]] = sorted(exponents.items())

    def walk(index: int, value: int, mpf: int) -> Iterable[Tuple[int, int]]:
        if index == len(items):
            yield value, mpf
            return
        p, e = items[index]
        power = 1
        for exponent in range(e + 1):
            yield from walk(index + 1, value * power,
                            p if exponent > 0 else mpf)
            power *= p

    return walk(0, 1, 0)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Demonstration blocks
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def verify_trace_law(b1: int = 30) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Check `n | K(B1,y) <==> P+(n) <= y` on every divisor n of K(B1,B1) and
    every schedule cut y.  Returns (checks_done, failures)."""
    cuts: List[int] = [0] + primes_up_to(b1)
    partial: Dict[int, int] = {y: stage_product(b1, y) for y in cuts}
    checks = 0
    failures = 0
    for n, mpf in divisors_with_max_prime(stage_exponents(b1, b1)):
        for y in cuts:
            lhs = partial[y] % n == 0
            rhs = mpf <= y
            checks += 1
            if lhs != rhs:
                failures += 1
    return checks, failures


def firing_index_statistics(n_max: int) -> Dict[str, float]:
    """Empirical distribution of the normalized firing index
    pi(P+(n)) / pi(N) for n uniform in (0, N], with the stage-one bound
    B1 = N.  Returns median, mean, final-20% tail mass and first-20% mass."""
    primes = primes_up_to(n_max)
    lpf = largest_prime_factor_table(n_max)
    total_steps = len(primes)
    # rank[p] = pi(p) for prime p; built once
    rank: Dict[int, int] = {p: i + 1 for i, p in enumerate(primes)}
    indices: List[float] = []
    for n in range(2, n_max + 1):
        indices.append(rank[lpf[n]] / total_steps)
    indices.sort()
    count = len(indices)
    median = indices[count // 2]
    mean = sum(indices) / count
    tail = sum(1 for x in indices if x > 0.8) / count
    head = sum(1 for x in indices if x <= 0.2) / count
    return {
        "N": float(n_max),
        "steps": float(total_steps),
        "median": median,
        "mean": mean,
        "final_20pct_mass": tail,
        "first_20pct_mass": head,
    }


def exact_late_tail(m: int, b1: int, y: int) -> int:
    """Exact number of integers n in (0, M] whose firing position exceeds y,
    i.e. that are divisible by some prime in (y, B1].  For M <= y^2 no integer
    can carry two such primes, so this equals sum_{y < p <= B1} floor(M/p)."""
    late_primes = [p for p in primes_up_to(b1) if p > y]
    return sum(m // p for p in late_primes)


def divisor_model_late_factor(b1: int, y: int) -> int:
    """prod_{y < p <= B1} (floor(log_p B1) + 1): the exact factor by which the
    divisor count of the full stage-one multiplier exceeds that of the partial
    product at cut y.  The divisor model therefore fires *late* with
    probability 1 - 1/factor."""
    factor = 1
    for p in primes_up_to(b1):
        if p > y:
            factor *= int(math.log(b1) / math.log(p) + 1e-12) + 1
    return factor


def collision_probability(p: int, k: int) -> float:
    """1 - (1 - 1/p)^k: the chance that k guarded group operations modulo p
    accidentally hit a multiple of p, independently of the point's order.
    Evaluated as -expm1(k * log1p(-1/p)) so it stays accurate for huge p."""
    return -math.expm1(k * math.log1p(-1.0 / p))


def late_density_log_bound(b1: int, y: int) -> float:
    """The unconditional structural cap 2*B1 / (y * floor(log2 y)) on the
    fraction of orders that can fire after schedule position y."""
    return 2.0 * b1 / (y * math.floor(math.log2(y)))


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Driver
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def banner(text: str) -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 78)
    print(text)
    print("=" * 78)


def main() -> None:
    banner("1.  THE TRACE LAW:  n | K(B1, y)  <==>  P+(n) <= y")
    for b1 in (12, 20, 30):
        checks, failures = verify_trace_law(b1)
        print(f"  B1 = {b1:>3}:  {checks:>6} (divisor, cut) pairs checked, "
              f"{failures} violations")
    print("  The firing moment of a stage-one reachable order depends on nothing")
    print("  except its largest prime factor.")

    banner("2.  THE FIRING INDEX PILES UP NEAR ZERO")
    print(f"  {'N':>9} {'steps':>7} {'median':>9} {'mean':>9} "
          f"{'final 20%':>10} {'first 20%':>10}")
    for exponent in (3, 4, 5, 6):
        stats = firing_index_statistics(10**exponent)
        print(f"  {int(stats['N']):>9} {int(stats['steps']):>7} "
              f"{stats['median']:>9.3f} {stats['mean']:>9.3f} "
              f"{stats['final_20pct_mass']:>10.3f} "
              f"{stats['first_20pct_mass']:>10.3f}")
    print("  A uniform firing index would print 0.500 / 0.500 / 0.200 / 0.200.")
    print("  Instead the median collapses toward 0 and the late tail decays.")

    banner("3.  THE EXACT LATE TAIL AT B1 = 100, CUT AT y = 67")
    late = exact_late_tail(4489, 100, 67)
    print(f"  Late schedule primes (last six of the 25 steps): "
          f"{[p for p in primes_up_to(100) if p > 67]}")
    print(f"  Integers in (0, 67^2 = 4489] that fire in that window: {late}")
    print(f"  Density = {late}/4489 = {late / 4489:.4f}")
    print(f"  Reciprocal cap  sum_{{67<p<=100}} 1/p = "
          f"{sum(1 / p for p in primes_up_to(100) if p > 67):.4f} < 2/25 = 0.08")
    print("  Uniformity over the final 24% of the schedule would demand ~0.24.")

    banner("4.  THE COMPETING DIVISOR NULL MODEL FIRES *LATE*")
    factor = divisor_model_late_factor(100, 67)
    full_tau = divisor_count(stage_exponents(100, 100))
    part_tau = divisor_count(stage_exponents(100, 67))
    print(f"  tau(K(100,100)) = {full_tau},  tau(K(100,67)) = {part_tau}")
    print(f"  ratio = {full_tau // part_tau}, predicted factor "
          f"prod_(67<p<=100)(floor(log_p 100)+1) = {factor}")
    print(f"  Divisor model late mass  = {1 - 1 / factor:.4f}  (~98%)")
    print(f"  Integer model late cap   = {2 / 25:.4f}  (8%)")
    print("  The two null models differ by more than a factor of twelve on the")
    print("  very quantity the experiment measured.")

    banner("5.  LIKELIHOOD OF THE OBSERVED EMPTY TAIL (0 hits out of 55)")
    uniform_likelihood = (4 / 5) ** 55
    structural_likelihood = (23 / 25) ** 55
    print(f"  Under the pre-registered uniform law (tail = 20%):   "
          f"{uniform_likelihood:.3e}")
    print(f"  Under the structural cap (tail <= 8%):               "
          f"{structural_likelihood:.3e}")
    print(f"  Likelihood ratio: {structural_likelihood / uniform_likelihood:.1f} "
          f"in favour of the structural law")
    print(f"  Under the divisor model (tail = 63/64):              "
          f"{(1 / 64) ** 55:.3e}  (annihilated)")

    banner("6.  THE COLLISION BASELINE IS A CEILING, AND IT IS SCALE FREE")
    print(f"  {'bit length':>11} {'p (approx)':>14} {'k = 2.59*B1':>14} "
          f"{'1-(1-1/p)^k':>13} {'ceiling k/p':>12}")
    for bits in (26, 32, 48, 64):
        p = 2 ** (bits - 1) + 1
        b1 = int(0.125 * p)
        k = int(2.59 * b1)
        print(f"  {bits:>11} {p:>14} {k:>14} "
              f"{collision_probability(p, k):>13.4f} {k / p:>12.4f}")
    print("  The ceiling depends only on the ratio k/p, so it does NOT decay with")
    print("  bit length: a collision-dominated account cannot predict a collapse.")
    print("  Measured success rates: 65.0% (bitlen 26) and 62.5% (bitlen 32),")
    print("  against a ceiling of 0.324 -- an excess of about 0.30.")

    banner("7.  PIGEONHOLE: GENUINE ORDER-HITS MUST EXIST")
    successes, curves = 25, 40
    max_collisions = math.floor(0.324 * curves)
    print(f"  Cell: {curves} curves, {successes} successes.")
    print(f"  At most floor(0.324 * {curves}) = {max_collisions} can be collisions.")
    print(f"  Hence at least {successes - max_collisions} successes are genuine "
          f"order-hits.")

    banner("8.  THE LATE TAIL VANISHES AS B1 GROWS (UNCONDITIONAL BOUND)")
    print(f"  {'B1':>10} {'cut y = B1/2':>13} {'cap 2B1/(y log2 y)':>21} "
          f"{'4/log2 y':>11}")
    for exponent in (10, 14, 20, 26, 32):
        b1 = 2**exponent
        y = 2 ** (exponent - 1)
        print(f"  {b1:>10} {y:>13} {late_density_log_bound(b1, y):>21.4f} "
              f"{4 / math.floor(math.log2(y)):>11.4f}")
    print("  A constant-fraction (20%) late tail is impossible for large B1.")

    banner("9.  MERTENS HEURISTIC FOR THE TAIL")
    print("  Conjecture: the mass firing in the final fraction tau of the")
    print("  schedule is  log(1/(1-tau)) / log(B1) * (1 + o(1)).")
    print(f"  {'B1':>10} {'predicted tail(0.2)':>21} {'measured':>10}")
    measured = {1000: 0.034, 10000: 0.024, 100000: 0.019, 1000000: 0.015}
    for b1, obs in measured.items():
        predicted = math.log(1 / 0.8) / math.log(b1)
        print(f"  {b1:>10} {predicted:>21.4f} {obs:>10.4f}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

  ]
}

You are evaluating a batch of candidate mathematical conjectures.

For EACH direction, judge it on its own mathematical merit:

  - Is it non-trivial, well-defined, and mathematically fruitful?

  - Is it actionable — can it lead to real theorems and proofs?

  - Is it original, or redundant with known results?

You DECIDE which directions to KEEP and which to PURGE. There is NO
fixed number of either: keep every direction that is genuinely worth
pursuing and purge every direction that is trivial, redundant,
ill-defined, or unproductive. Depending on the batch, you may keep
all 10, purge all 10, or anything in

            ## v19 Research Core Methodology — Speculative Scientific-Method Loop

You are the Principal Investigator leading a speculative research team with four
roles: **Hypothesizer**, **Experimenter**, **Analyst**, and **Critic**. This engine
is configured for **Speculative Specifying (Bold Conjectures)**: target high-risk,
high-reward, grand-challenge level research while maintaining adversarial rigor.

### Stage 1 — Hypothesize (team: Hypothesizer)
Brainstorm 5–7 falsifiable conjectures about the topic. At least three must be
bold, surprising, or grand-challenge level. Rank them by expected scientific
impact, not by ease of proof.
**CRITICAL SCORING REQUIREMENT**: To maximize your Phase A quality score, your
conjectures MUST aim for extreme `proof_depth` (deep structural hierarchies rather
than shallow one-liners) and `cross_domain` bridging (combining distinct areas of
math, e.g., algebra with topology, or geometry with combinatorics).

### Stage 2 — Experiment (team: Experimenter)
For each conjecture, attempt to prove it in Lean 4 or disprove it with a concrete
counterexample. Prioritize the boldest conjectures first. If a proof is beyond
reach, prove the strongest lemma you can and mark the remaining step with exactly
one `sorry` that is clearly documented.

### Stage 3 — Analyze (team: Analyst)
Summarize what survived, what failed, and **why** failures failed. Distinguish
"true but hard", "false", and "needs a different definition". Extract structural
patterns that could unify several observations.

### Stage 4 — Critique / Adversarial Review (team: Critic)
Before finalizing, challenge every theorem:
- Is any theorem trivial (True, definitional equality, `native_decide`)?
- Does every main theorem have 0 sorries?
- Do the results genuinely extend the attached catalog files?
- Are there hidden assumptions or corner cases that break the claim?
If you find a weakness, fix it or replace the theorem with a guarded version and
explain the boundary.

### Stage 5 — Synthesize (team: Principal Investigator)
Combine the verified results into clean, compiling Lean 4 files.
Write a `FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md` that lists 3–5 **bold, testable** conjectures
derived from Stage 3 and Stage 4. Each conjecture must include a
"The key insight is..." sentence and a "Why now?" justification.

array named future_directions.json with one object per direction

When the research team comes together with results, do not stop. Treat the
synthesized findings as the next problem statement and immediately run the full
scientific-method loop again: hypothesize, experiment, review, synthesize,
critique. Repeat this cycle continuously within the available context window,

# Phase A Research Mission v19c: Parallel residual blocks obey a tensor-product certificate

            ## Assignment
            **Domain**: Algebra | **Mode**: team
            **Description**: In the cartesian monoidal category of real normed spaces and Lipschitz maps, parallel residual blocks with residual constants `K₁` and `K₂` have Lipschitz constant at most `max (1 + K₁) (1 + K₂)` for the max product norm, and this bound is attained for every `K₁,K₂ ≥ 0`. A counterexample to either the upper bound or attainability falsifies the conjecture.
            **Mathematical Framing**: In the cartesian monoidal category of real normed spaces and Lipschitz maps, parallel residual blocks with residual constants `K₁` and `K₂` have Lipschitz constant at most `max (1 + K₁) (1 + K₂)` for the max product norm, and this bound is attained for every `K₁,K₂ ≥ 0`. A counterexample to either the upper bound or attainability falsifies the conjecture.



            ## v19 Research Core Methodology — Speculative Scientific-Method Loop

You are the Principal Investigator leading a speculative research team with four
roles: **Hypothesizer**, **Experimenter**, **Analyst**, and **Critic**. This engine
is configured for **Speculative Specifying (Bold Conjectures)**: target high-risk,
high-reward, grand-challenge level research while maintaining adversarial rigor.

### Stage 1 — Hypothesize (team: Hypothesizer)
Brainstorm 5–7 falsifiable conjectures about the topic. At least three must be
bold, surprising, or grand-challenge level. Rank them by expected scientific
impact, not by ease of proof.
**CRITICAL SCORING REQUIREMENT**: To maximize your Phase A quality score, your
conjectures MUST aim for extreme `proof_depth` (deep structural hierarchies rather
than shallow one-liners) and `cross_domain` bridging (combining distinct areas of
math, e.g., algebra with topology, or geometry with combinatorics).

### Stage 2 — Experiment (team: Experimenter)
For each conjecture, attempt to prove it in Lean 4 or disprove it with a concrete
counterexample. Prioritize the boldest conjectures first. If a proof is beyond
reach, prove the strongest lemma you can and mark the remaining step with exactly
one `sorry` that is clearly documented.

### Stage 3 — Analyze (team: Analyst)
Summarize what survived, what failed, and **why** failures failed. Distinguish
"true but hard", "false", and "needs a different definition". Extract structural
patterns that could unify several observations.

### Stage 4 — Critique / Adversarial Review (team: Critic)
Before finalizing, challenge every theorem:
- Is any theorem trivial (True, definitional equality, `native_decide`)?
- Does every main theorem have 0 sorries?
- Do the results genuinely extend the attached catalog files?
- Are there hidden assumptions or corner cases that break the claim?
If you find a weakness, fix it or replace the theorem with a guarded version and
explain the boundary.

### Stage 5 — Synthesize (team: Principal Investigator)
Combine the verified results into clean, compiling Lean 4 files.
Write a `FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md` that lists 3–5 **bold, testable** conjectures
derived from Stage 3 and Stage 4. Each conjecture must include a
"The key insight is..." sentence and a "Why now?" justification.

ADDITIONALLY — machine-readable directions block (REQUIRED). In
FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md, after the prose sections, emit a fenced JSON
array named future_directions.json with one object per direction
(3–6 entries), each with exactly these keys:
```json
[{"title": "<short noun-phrase name, NOT a sentence>",
  "domain": "<one of: NumberTheory, Algebra, Geometry, Combinatorics, Computation, Physics, Probability, Cryptography, Logic, MachineLearning, Tropical, Bridges>",
  "description": "<2-4 sentences: the conjecture, the approach, why it matters>",
  "conjecture": "<the precise mathematical claim>",
  "test": "<how to test or formalize it>",
  "if_true": "<consequence if true>",
  "if_false": "<consequence if false>",
  "proof_strategy": "<sketch of the proof route>",
  "catalog_references": ["<Catalog.lean.module>"]}]

Titles must be noun phrases ("Silver-Ratio Spectral Gap for Pell Spines"),
never sentences or recaps ("This cycle proved..." is forbidden).

### Perpetual Scientific Iteration (do not stop at first synthesis)
When the research team comes together with results, do not stop. Treat the
synthesized findings as the next problem statement and immediately run the full
scientific-method loop again: hypothesize, experiment, review, synthesize,
critique. Repeat this cycle continuously within the available context window,
refining, deepening, and cross-checking until forced to emit output. Use
Aristotle to its fullest.

### Anti-Trivial Guardrails
- Do not produce trivial proofs (`True := by trivial`, `rfl`-only, `Inhabited X`-only, `native_decide`-only).
- Use an insight-bearing tactic (e.g. `induction`, `nlinarith`, `omega`, `field_simp`).

### Self-Critique Checklist
- No theorem is trivial.
- Every main theorem has 0 sorries.
- Lab Notes blocks contain real experimental data.

### Strictly Forbidden in Phase A
Do NOT create packaging deliverables in Phase A: `ARTICLE.md`, `RESEARCH_PAPER.md`, `demo.py`, `PACKAGE.json`.

### Recursive Abduction / Thread Continuation (v19c)
If prior-cycle context is provided, treat it as a live research thread: refine
the hypotheses from the previous cycle, attempt to close open conjectures, and
produce three concrete next-cycle sub-conjectures. If no prior context is
provided, still run a self-contained abductive loop: generate conjectures, test
them, and immediately spin off the most promising follow-up conjectures as
future directions.


            ## Hard Constraints
            1. Every theorem MUST be fully proved (0 sorries, no stubbed signatures).
            2. No circular proofs (a theorem must never reference itself directly or transitively in its proof).
            3. No trivial results (e.g. `True := by trivial`, `rfl`-only, `native_decide`-only).
            4. All files must be self-contained and compilable with Lean 4 (mathlib4 v4.28.0).
            5. Build directly on existing catalog definitions — do not re-invent.

            ## Output Requirements
            Return ONLY:
            1. `.lean` files in `Catalog/Algebra/` with complete formal proofs.
            2. `FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md` with 3–5 concrete, falsifiable conjectures derived from your findings.
            3. `SELF_EVALUATION.json` with your honest self-assessment of the research:
               {
                 "quality_score": <float 0.0 to 1.0>,
                 "proof_depth": <float 0.0 to 1.0>,
                 "novelty": <float 0.0 to 1.0>,
                 "grade": "world_class" | "substantial" | "partial" | "shallow" | "trivial",
                 "rationale": "<2-3 sentence justification of grade and mathematical significance>"
               }

            Focus all compute budget on proving theorems.


### Computational Evidence Stage (Recommended)

Before writing the formal Lean 4 proof, you are strongly encouraged to produce
computational evidence for the claim. Create a file named `ComputationalEvidence.md`
in the project directory with:

1. **Small-case calculations** — compute the first several instances of the object/conjecture.
2. **OEIS search results** — if a sequence appears, note its OEIS ID and first terms.
3. **Counterexample hunt** — test the universal claim on a representative sample; report any counterexample found.
4. **Plots or tables** — include any relevant visual/numerical data.

If you choose to skip this stage, you MUST explicitly justify why computational
evidence is unnecessary or infeasible in a `SkipEvidenceJustification.md` file.

Do not let the evidence stage dominate the project; keep it concise and directly
relevant to the theorem you intend to prove.
